nuance.usage_note: Americans use incommensurability mainly in philosophy of science, ethics and mathematics. In everyday talk they would say the two things are 'apples and oranges' or 'impossible to compare'. Using the word in a casual setting would sound overly academic.

distinctions.note: Incomparability is a looser term for things that cannot be meaningfully compared, while incommensurability is a precise term for having no common measure.
Irrationality in mathematics means a number cannot be written as a ratio of integers, which is one specific case of incommensurability.

examples.everyday: I can't really compare the two jobs because the pay and the lifestyle are so different that it's almost incommensurability.
examples.professional: The team faced an incommensurability problem, because the cost data and the customer satisfaction scores had no common unit.
examples.analytical: Kuhn's account of scientific revolutions raised the question of whether rival theories share enough meaning to make their incommensurability a real barrier to comparison.

nuance.analogy: Like trying to measure a length with a clock: the two scales share nothing, so no comparison is possible.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin incommensurabilis, from in- 'not' plus commensurabilis 'measurable together'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, such as putting primary stress on the first syllable.
Using incommensurability in casual talk where comparability or apples and oranges would sound more natural.

senses.definition: A Calvinist who holds that election is a logical consequent of the Fall of man in the original divine plan.

core.definition: A Calvinist who holds that God decided to elect some people after, not before, planning for the Fall of humanity.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on SAIR, the fourth syllable, and the secondary stress is on the first syllable. The final "-ian" is weak and sounds like "un."

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise label within Reformed theology and sounds technical to most people.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly use this term in seminary, theology, or historical discussions of Calvinism. In everyday church talk people rarely use it, and they might instead explain the view in plain words. Its opposite, supralapsarian, is used in the same academic settings.

distinctions.note: A supralapsarian holds that God decreed the elect and reprobate before deciding to permit the Fall, while an infralapsarian places the decree after the Fall.
An Arminian rejects unconditional election, while an infralapsarian is a Calvinist who affirms it.

examples.everyday: My pastor is an infralapsarian, so he thinks God planned redemption after foreseeing the Fall.
examples.professional: In the seminar I teach, we compare the supralapsarian and infralapsarian positions on predestination.
examples.analytical: The infralapsarian argues that the decree of election presupposes the fall of humanity as a logically prior condition.

nuance.analogy: An infralapsarian is like an architect who sketches the house after noticing the storm damage, while a supralapsarian sketches it before the storm.
nuance.etymology: From Latin infra 'below, after' and lapsus 'fall,' plus -arian.
common_mistakes: Using the term for all Calvinists; only those who take the infralapsarian position on the decrees qualify.
Mispronouncing the stress, saying in-fruh-LAP-sair-ee-un instead of in-fruh-lap-SAIR-ee-un.

senses.definition: In an innocent manner.

core.definition: In a way that is not meant to cause harm, wrong, or offense; without bad intent.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle vowels are reduced, and the final -ly is a light, quick 'lee' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it usually excuses a mistake or describes a harmless action.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'innocently' to say that someone did something without bad intent, such as 'she innocently asked a personal question'. It often softens a small error. In legal contexts, 'innocently' can also mean without knowledge of wrongdoing, as in 'innocently acquired property'.

distinctions.note: 'Naively' suggests a lack of judgment or experience, while 'innocently' suggests no harmful intent.
'Accidentally' refers to an unplanned event, while 'innocently' focuses on the lack of bad intent behind an action.

examples.everyday: My little boy innocently asked the cashier if she was married, and she just laughed.
examples.professional: Someone innocently changed the config file, which broke the deployment for half the team.
examples.analytical: The author innocently assumes that good intentions alone can justify the policy's effects.

nuance.analogy: Acting innocently is like stepping on a wet floor without seeing the sign: you did not mean to cause trouble.
nuance.etymology: From 'innocent' (Latin 'innocens', not harmful) with the adverb ending '-ly'.
common_mistakes: Using 'innocently' to mean 'innocently guilty', which is contradictory.
Pronouncing the middle vowel too strongly; it is weak in American speech.

senses.definition: A joke that is understood or meant to be understood only by certain people who are aware of the details (an ingroup).
senses.example: After the incident with the potato peeler, references to potatoes became an inside joke among the witnesses.

core.definition: A joke that only a particular group of people understands, because they share knowledge of the background or details.

pronunciation.tip: In American speech, a compound noun like this puts the main stress on the first word, IN, and the second word, JOKE, gets a lighter but clear stress. Say it fast as one phrase: 'IN-side JOHK'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or friendly. It signals closeness and belonging, but it can also feel exclusive to outsiders.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'inside joke' in casual conversation with friends, coworkers or families, often to explain a laugh that others don't get. A natural reply is 'Oh, sorry, it's an inside joke' or 'You had to be there.' It is informal, so avoid it in formal writing.

distinctions.note: Private joke is nearly identical and sounds a bit more personal. Inside joke is the more common phrase in American English.
A running joke is repeated over time within a group. An inside joke may happen only once and rely on shared knowledge.

examples.everyday: Sorry, that was an inside joke with my roommates about the broken microwave.
examples.professional: The team has an inside joke about 'the staging server,' so don't take it too seriously in the meeting.
examples.analytical: Inside jokes function as a boundary marker, signaling membership in a group by excluding those who lack the shared context.

nuance.analogy: An inside joke is like a secret handshake: only people who know the signal can take part.
nuance.etymology: Inside derives from Old English innan, within; joke from Latin iocus, jest.
common_mistakes: Saying 'inside joke' with equal stress on both words, which sounds flat; the first word should be stronger.
Using it for a joke that is simply hard to understand; it implies shared knowledge among a group.

conversation.text: Sorry, it's an inside joke. You kind of had to be there.
"Why do you all keep saying 'pineapple'?" "Oh, it's an inside joke from our trip."
My sister and I have so many inside jokes that nobody else understands.

senses.definition: The state of being insignificant.

core.definition: The quality of being too small, minor, or unimportant to have any real effect or value.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on NIF, and the vowel in the last syllables is a reduced schwa. Learners often pronounce the middle 'nif' with a long EE sound and stress the wrong syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes something as trivial or of little worth, and it can sting when applied to a person's contribution or feelings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in serious discussions, news, and personal reflection about feeling small or unimportant, as in 'a sense of insignificance.' In casual talk people more often say 'it doesn't matter' or 'it's no big deal.' The adjective 'insignificant' is more common in everyday speech.

distinctions.note: Unimportance is a plainer, everyday word for lacking importance; insignificance is more formal and often stresses that something has almost no effect at all.
Triviality focuses on something being petty or small-minded in content, while insignificance focuses on having little measurable or meaningful effect.

examples.everyday: After the big storm, I felt a strange insignificance standing next to all that wreckage.
examples.professional: The team agreed that the change in latency was within the margin of error, so the insignificance of the result meant we would not roll it out.
examples.analytical: Pascal's image of the thinking reed captures a tension between human insignificance in the cosmos and the dignity of human reason.

nuance.analogy: Like a single grain of sand on a huge beach: real, but hard to notice.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin insignificantia, from in- 'not' plus significare 'to signify.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, saying 'in-sig-NIF-i-cance' with a long i in the final part.
Using 'insignificance' when 'unimportance' would be more natural in everyday conversation.

senses.definition: To cover with large amounts of water; to flood.
senses.example: The Dutch would sometimes inundate the land to hinder the Spanish army.

senses.definition: To overwhelm.
senses.example: The agency was inundated with phone calls.

core.definition: To flood a place with water, or to overwhelm someone with a large amount of something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, IN. The second syllable is a reduced uh, and the final -date rhymes with late.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It describes an overwhelming amount, often unwelcome.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use inundate for overwhelming volumes of email, requests, or customers, and for floods. In casual talk people more often say 'we're swamped' or 'I'm buried in work.' The verb is often used in the passive: 'we were inundated with calls.'

distinctions.note: Flood is more common and everyday for water or large quantities. Inundate sounds more formal and suggests being overwhelmed.
Overwhelm focuses on the emotional effect on a person. Inundate focuses on a large amount arriving all at once.

examples.everyday: Sorry I'm late, I got inundated with texts from my sister this morning.
examples.professional: Our support team was inundated with tickets after the outage, so we added temporary staff.
examples.analytical: Modern readers are inundated with information, which makes selection more important than access.

nuance.analogy: To inundate is to pour a bucket of water into a small cup until it overflows everywhere.
nuance.etymology: From Latin inundare, to flood over, from in- 'into' and undare 'to rise in waves', from unda 'wave'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable, as in in-un-DATE.
Using 'inundated of' instead of 'inundated with'.

inundate.etymology: Latin *inundātus*, the perfect passive participle of *inundō* (“to flood, overflow”) (see *-ate*), from *in-* + *undō* (“to overflow, wave”), from *unda* (“wave”) + *-ō*.

senses.definition: In an inventive manner.

core.definition: In a clever, original way that shows new ideas or creative thinking.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the VEN syllable. The -ive ending is short, and the final -ly is a clear 'lee' sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises the creative way something is done.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use inventively mostly in writing, reviews and formal speech, often about how someone handles a problem or designs something. In casual talk, people more often say 'in a clever way' or 'creatively'. It sounds slightly formal, so it fits a work review or an article better than a chat with friends.

distinctions.note: Creatively is more common in everyday speech and can refer to art or any expressive activity; inventively stresses new practical ideas.
Cleverly can suggest cunning or a trick, while inventively is purely positive and focuses on originality.

examples.everyday: My sister inventively used old pallets to build a bookshelf for her apartment.
examples.professional: The engineer inventively reused the existing sensors to monitor the new system without extra hardware.
examples.analytical: The novel inventively blends historical records with invented letters to question what counts as evidence.

nuance.analogy: Working inventively is like a jazz musician who builds a new melody from a familiar tune.
nuance.etymology: From inventive (from Late Latin inventivus) plus the adverb ending -ly, from Latin invenire, to find.
common_mistakes: Using inventively to mean 'imaginatively' in a fictional or dishonest sense; for lies, Americans say 'made up' or 'fabricated'.
Stressing the wrong syllable, saying in-ven-TIVE-ly instead of in-VEN-tiv-lee.

senses.definition: A long speech or prose work that bitterly laments the state of society and its morals, and often contains a prophecy of its coming downfall.

core.definition: A long, bitter complaint about society's moral decline, often predicting that it will soon be punished or collapse.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the -MY- syllable, which is the most prominent part of the word. The final -iad is a reduced schwa, so it sounds like -ud, not like the word add.

nuance.connotation: Negative, because it describes a gloomy, complaining speech or text; sometimes used with a touch of humor for a dramatic rant.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use jeremiad mainly in writing, in essays, political commentary, and book reviews, to describe a long lament about the state of the country or of morals. It is not common in casual speech. You might say he delivered a jeremiad about the younger generation, which signals a somewhat condescending or exaggerated tone. In conversation, people more often say rant or lecture.

distinctions.note: A rant is an angry, unstructured outburst, while a jeremiad is a more organized and prophetic lament that ends with a warning of doom.
A sermon is any religious talk meant to teach or exhort, while a jeremiad is specifically a gloomy denunciation that predicts disaster.

examples.everyday: My uncle gave another jeremiad about how nobody writes letters anymore.
examples.professional: The op-ed read as a jeremiad about the company's declining morale, but it offered no concrete fixes.
examples.analytical: Puritan sermons often took the form of a jeremiad, lamenting the colony's sins and warning of divine judgment.

nuance.analogy: A jeremiad is like a stormy weather forecast delivered as a sermon: it spends most of its time on how bad things are and promises that the sky will fall.
nuance.etymology: From French jérémiade, from Jérémie, the French form of Jeremiah, the Hebrew prophet whose book is full of laments and warnings.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as JER-uh-mysd, instead of the middle -MY- syllable.
Using jeremiad as a casual word for any complaint; it implies a long, serious and gloomy speech with a prophecy of doom.
nuance.biblical_note: The word comes from the prophet Jeremiah, whose Hebrew name is Yirmeyahu, meaning 'the LORD exalts' or 'the LORD throws'. Jeremiah is known for warning Judah that its sins would bring Babylonian conquest, and he is traditionally credited with the Book of Lamentations, which mourns the fall of Jerusalem. Because of these themes, his name became the source of the word for a lament that predicts downfall.

jeremiad.etymology: From French *jérémiade*, from *Jérémie*, from Latin *Ieremias*, from Hebrew *ירמיה* (“Jeremiah”). who lamented the moral state of Judah and predicted her downfall.

senses.definition: Cheerful and good-humored; jolly, merry.

core.definition: Cheerful, friendly and good-humored, often in a warm, jolly way that makes other people feel at ease.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, JOH. The second and third syllables are weak, so the ending sounds like 'vee-ul' with a reduced vowel. Do not stress the final syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it describes a warm, friendly temperament. It can sound slightly old-fashioned or a little exaggerated when used of someone who is merely polite.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use jovial to describe a person who is warmly cheerful, often a host, a coach or a boss who jokes around with people. It is more descriptive than casual, so you would say 'He's a jovial guy' rather than using it as a greeting. A natural reply might be to agree with a laugh, such as 'He really is.'

distinctions.note: Jolly is more informal and playful, and can describe a whole mood, while jovial emphasizes a warm, sociable temperament in a person.
Cheerful is a general word for being happy, while jovial adds a sense of hearty humor and sociability.

examples.everyday: Our neighbor is so jovial that he waves at everyone on the street and tells jokes at the mailbox.
examples.professional: Our project lead has a jovial manner that keeps the stand-up meetings from feeling tense.
examples.analytical: Dickens often gives his jovial characters a warmth that contrasts with the cruelty of the institutions around them.

nuance.analogy: A jovial person is like a warm fireplace on a cold day: people gather near them because they feel good being there.
nuance.etymology: From Latin Jovialis, 'of Jupiter,' and in English from the belief that people born under the planet Jupiter were cheerful.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'JOE-vee-al' with a long final syllable.
Confusing it with 'jovial' meaning 'serious' or 'solemn,' which is the opposite.
Using 'jovially' as an adjective, as in 'a jovially man.'

senses.definition: A measure of "heaviness of the tails" of a probability distribution, defined as the fourth cumulant divided by the square of the variance of the probability distribution.
Excess kurtosis: the difference between a given distribution's kurtosis and the kurtosis of a normal distribution.

core.definition: In statistics, a measure of how heavy the tails of a probability distribution are, compared with a normal distribution.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, TOH. The first syllable is an r-colored schwa, so say 'kur,' not 'kur-ta' with a clear t; the t is light and close to a d.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Kurtosis is a technical term used in statistics, data science, finance and quantitative research. Americans say it in analysis meetings, papers and model reviews, often with 'excess kurtosis' to compare against a normal distribution. In casual talk it would sound unusually specialized.

distinctions.note: Skewness measures asymmetry of a distribution, while kurtosis measures how heavy the tails are and how peaked the center is.
Variance measures spread around the mean; kurtosis describes the shape of the tails, which variance alone does not reveal.

examples.everyday: My friend who works in finance said the returns looked weird because they had high kurtosis.
examples.professional: Before we trust the model, let's check the kurtosis of the residuals to see whether outliers are skewing the errors.
examples.analytical: Excess kurtosis, defined relative to the normal distribution, quantifies the tail weight that a variance estimate alone cannot capture.

nuance.analogy: If variance tells you how wide a crowd is, kurtosis tells you how many people are standing far off at the edges.
nuance.etymology: From Greek kyrtos, meaning curved or bulging.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as KUR-tuh-sis instead of kur-TOH-sis.
Confusing kurtosis with skewness, which measures asymmetry rather than tail weight.

kurtosis.etymology: (published 1899 in "On certain Properties of the Hypergeometrical Series, and so on the fitting of such series to Observation Polygons in the Theory of Chance", Phil.

core.definition: A title for Jesus Christ, based on John the Baptist's words that Jesus is the sacrificial lamb who takes away the sin of the world.

pronunciation.tip: Stress LAM and GAHD, and reduce 'of' to a weak 'uhv'. Americans say the phrase quickly with the words linked together.

nuance.connotation: Positive and reverent; it is used in worship, prayer and theology, and it can sound too churchy in casual conversation outside faith settings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often hear this phrase in church, in hymns and in the Mass or communion liturgy. In everyday conversation people use it when talking about faith or a Bible passage, not as a casual expression. Protestant, Catholic and Orthodox Christians all recognize the title, so it is safe in mixed religious settings.

distinctions.note: The Paschal lamb is the Passover lamb sacrificed in Exodus 12, which the title Lamb of God echoes, but the phrase names Christ.
The Good Shepherd emphasizes Christ as one who guides and protects, while Lamb of God emphasizes his sacrificial death.

collocations: Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world

examples.everyday: My grandmother sang the Lamb of God hymn every Sunday, and she still hums it when she cooks.
examples.professional: In my sermon on John 1:29, I will explain why the Lamb of God title connects Jesus to the Passover.
examples.analytical: John's Lamb of God title draws together the Passover imagery of Exodus and the suffering servant of Isaiah 53.

nuance.analogy: The title is like a family name that connects a new story to an old tradition of sacrifice.
nuance.etymology: From the Latin Agnus Dei, the wording of John 1:29 in the Vulgate.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'of' fully as 'off' instead of the reduced 'uhv'.
Using the phrase casually as a comment on someone's innocence, which sounds strange outside religious talk.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word amnos (lamb) appears in John 1:29 and 1:36, where John the Baptist calls Jesus the Lamb of God that takes away the sin of the world. The image links to the Passover lamb of Exodus 12, whose blood marked the Israelite homes. Isaiah 53:7 describes a servant led like a lamb to the slaughter, and 1 Peter 1:19 speaks of Christ as a lamb without blemish. Revelation 5:6 pictures a Lamb standing as though it had been slain.

senses.definition: Synonym of lapidary.
Synonym of lapidary.

core.definition: Relating to gems or to carved stone; a rare variant of lapidary, used mostly in literary writing.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on DAIR, the third syllable. The final -ian is a reduced unstressed syllable, so say it quickly as un.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive, suggesting precision and polish.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use lapidarian; they almost always say lapidary for both the adjective and the noun. You will mainly meet lapidarian in older or highly literary writing. In everyday speech, use lapidary.

distinctions.note: Lapidary is the standard, common form; lapidarian is a rarer variant with the same meaning.

examples.professional: The museum hired a lapidarian conservator to restore the carved stone panels.
examples.analytical: Her lapidarian prose seems carved rather than written, each sentence polished to a hard finish.

nuance.analogy: Like a gem cutter facet by facet, the word shapes stone into something precise.
nuance.etymology: From Latin lapidarius, of stones, from lapis, stone.
common_mistakes: Using lapidarian in ordinary conversation, where lapidary is the normal word.
Stressing the second syllable (-PAH-) instead of the third.

senses.definition: A variable that is not directly measured but is inferred by means of a mathematical model from one or more directly observed variables.

core.definition: A variable that cannot be measured directly but is inferred through a statistical model from several observed variables.

pronunciation.tip: Main stress is on VAIR in variable, and the final syllable is a weak 'bul'. Many learners say 'va-RI-able' with the stress wrong, so put the stress on the first syllable of VARIABLE.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, a technical term used in research and modeling.
nuance.usage_note: Statisticians, psychometricians and social scientists use this in methods discussions, for example when describing intelligence, anxiety or customer satisfaction measured through survey items. Americans rarely use it in casual conversation. In a meeting, you might say 'we treat engagement as a latent variable'.

distinctions.note: An observed variable is directly measured, while a latent variable is inferred from observed variables.
Hidden variable is used more in physics and philosophy of quantum mechanics, while latent variable is the standard term in statistics and machine learning.

examples.everyday: My friend says there is a hidden factor behind her sleep problems, a sort of latent variable like stress, that nobody has actually measured.
examples.professional: We cannot measure customer trust directly, so we treat it as a latent variable in the structural equation model.
examples.analytical: A latent variable is a theoretical construct whose values are inferred from the covariance among its observed indicators rather than observed themselves.

nuance.analogy: A latent variable is like the engine of a car: you cannot see it directly, but you infer it from how the car accelerates, sounds and handles.
nuance.etymology: 'Latent' comes from Latin latere, to lie hidden; 'variable' comes from Latin variabilis, changeable.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable in variable, saying vuh-RAY-bul instead of VAIR-ee-uh-bul.
Confusing latent with latest, which sounds similar but means most recent.

latent-variable.etymology: The variables are *latent* (“hidden”) because they are not directly observed, but instead inferred from other variables.

conversation.text: A latent variable is something we never observe directly but assume drives the data, like a user's taste.
Topic models treat each document's topic mixture as a latent variable.

senses.definition: To learn some skill requiring specialist knowledge.
To learn the basics or master introductory knowledge.
senses.example: Work slowly and cautiously until you have learned the ropes.

core.definition: To become familiar with how a new job, activity or system works, usually through practice and guidance.

pronunciation.tip: The is reduced to thuh before the consonant r, and the r in learn and ropes is American r-colored. Link the words so it sounds like LUR-nuh-ROHPS.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral; it describes a normal stage of getting started.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use learn the ropes for a new hire, student or volunteer who is adjusting to a workplace or activity. It is friendly and natural in both casual talk and professional settings. A common reply is 'Thanks, I'm still learning the ropes.' The phrase often comes with show someone the ropes.

distinctions.note: Get the hang of is a little more casual and emphasizes learning a knack, while learn the ropes emphasizes learning the routine and procedures of a job or place.
Master suggests complete expertise, while learn the ropes means getting to a basic working level.

collocations: learn the ropes at a new job

examples.everyday: I just started volunteering at the food bank, and the older volunteers are helping me learn the ropes.
examples.professional: The new hires are shadowing senior engineers for two weeks so they can learn the ropes before they take on tickets.
examples.analytical: Apprenticeship often works by learning the ropes through imitation, since much of the work is tacit rather than written down.

nuance.analogy: Learning the ropes is like a sailor learning which line controls which sail before the storm comes.
nuance.etymology: Often traced to sailing, where new sailors had to learn which ropes controlled the rigging.
common_mistakes: Saying learn the rope in the singular instead of the plural ropes.
Dropping the article as in learn ropes, which sounds unnatural.

learn-the-ropes.etymology: Of nautical origin: in the past, the phrase “he knows the ropes” written on a seaman’s discharge meant that he was inexperienced and familiar only with a ship’s principal ropes.

conversation.text: It'll take a few weeks to learn the ropes here.
I'm still learning the ropes at my new job.
Kevin will help you learn the ropes during your first month.

senses.definition: Of, pertaining to, or causing death; deadly; mortal; fatal.
Any weapon that causes death.
An allele that causes the death of the organism that carries it.
One of the higher alcohols of the paraffine series obtained from spermaceti as a white crystalline solid.

core.definition: Able to cause death; deadly or fatal, especially describing a dose, weapon, injury, or substance.

pronunciation.tip: The IPA in the item has a dot splitting the syllables, but the word is one stressed syllable followed by a reduced 'uhl,' so say LEE-thuhl. The 'th' is voiceless, as in 'thin,' and the final syllable is a syllabic l.

nuance.connotation: Negative and serious. It describes something that can kill, so it carries strong warning or danger.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in news, medicine, law, and science to describe things that can cause death, such as a lethal dose or a lethal weapon. In everyday speech, people more often say 'deadly' or 'fatal,' so 'lethal' sounds more formal or technical. It can also be used figuratively, as in 'a lethal combination,' but this is less common than the literal sense.

distinctions.note: Common and general, used both literally and for things that are very harmful or effective; 'lethal' is more technical and specific to causing death.
Describes an outcome or injury that ends in death, often used for accidents and diseases; 'lethal' describes something capable of causing death in general.
Literary or formal; it can mean subject to death or causing death, and is used in religious or poetic contexts.

examples.everyday: Doctors warned us that even a small amount of that cleaner could be lethal to a dog.
examples.professional: The security team flagged the drone as a potential lethal threat, so the protocol requires human review.
examples.analytical: The distinction between a lethal and a nonlethal intervention depends not only on intent but on the foreseeable consequences of the act.

nuance.analogy: It is like a switch that does not just hurt but completely stops the system from working.
nuance.etymology: From Latin letalis, from letum, meaning death.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'LEH-thal' with a short e, instead of the long ee in 'LEE-thuhl.'
Using 'lethal' for mildly harmful things, as in 'a lethal joke,' which sounds exaggerated unless used for humor.

senses.definition: The top or cover of a container.
A cap or hat.
One ounce of cannabis.
A motorcyclist's crash helmet.
In amateur radio, an incompetent operator.
Clipping of eyelid.
A hermetically sealed top piece on a microchip such as the integrated heat spreader on a CPU.
A restraint or control, as when "putting a lid" on something.
A kid (from the rhyming slang bin lid).
The sky.
One's mind.
An operculum or other lid-like cover.
To put a lid on (something).

core.definition: The removable top that covers a pot, jar, box, or other container.

pronunciation.tip: Use a short i as in 'sit', and end with a clear d sound. Do not add a vowel after it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes an everyday object without emotional weight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use lid for almost any cover that comes off a container: a pot lid, a jar lid, a coffee cup lid. In casual speech you may hear 'put a lid on it' to mean stop talking or stop an issue. In slang, lid can also mean one ounce of cannabis, so the word can sound drug-related in some settings. Context usually makes the everyday meaning clear.

distinctions.note: A cover can be any protective layer, while a lid is specifically the top of a container that opens and closes.
A cap usually screws or snaps onto a bottle or tube, while a lid lifts off or fits over a wide container.

examples.everyday: Can you put the lid on the soup so it stays warm while we wait?
examples.professional: The packaging team changed the lid design so the containers stack more easily on the shelf.
examples.analytical: Lévi-Strauss's distinction between cooked and raw suggests that a lid functions as a cultural boundary between what is kept in and what is shared.

nuance.analogy: A lid is like a door on a box: it closes what is inside and can be opened when you need it.
nuance.etymology: From Old English hlid, meaning a cover or gate.
common_mistakes: Using 'lid' for a bottle top; Americans usually say cap for bottles and tubes.
Saying 'put lid on' without 'the' or 'a' before lid.

lid.etymology: Middle English *lid*, *lyd*, from Old English *hlid*, from **hlid*, from Proto-Germanic **hlidą*, from Proto-Indo-European **ḱlitós* (“covered”), from Proto-Indo-European **ḱley-* (“to cover”).

conversation.text: Can I get a lid for my coffee? It's to go.
Make sure the lid is on tight before you drive.
This lid doesn't fit the cup.

senses.definition: Synonym of liquefy (“to make (something) into a liquid”); to liquidize.
To make (a sound) less harsh.
To use up (money or other assets) wastefully; to dissipate, to squander, to waste.
To kill (someone), usually violently, and especially for some ideological or political aim; to assassinate, to murder; also, to abolish or eliminate (something); to do away with, to put an end to.
To convert (assets) into cash; to encash, to realize, to redeem.
To settle (a debt) by paying the outstanding amount; to pay off.

To settle the financial affairs of (a corporation, partnership, or other business) with the aim of ceasing operations, by determining liabilities, using assets to pay debts, and apportioning the remaining assets if any; to wind up.
To resolve or settle (differences, disputes, etc.).
To ascertain (an amount of money), especially by agreement or through litigation; also, to set out (financial accounts) properly.
Of a corporation, partnership, or other business: to settle financial affairs with the aim of ceasing operations; to go into liquidation, to wind up.
senses.example: COVID-19 hit the company hard—I foresee it will liquidate within a year.

core.definition: To sell off a company's assets to pay its debts, or to close a business by converting everything into cash.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle syllable is a reduced 'wuh,' so the word is three syllables and not 'lik-wi-date' with a full vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in business and finance, but it can sound harsh in everyday talk. In crime fiction or informal slang it can mean to kill, which Americans recognize.
nuance.usage_note: In the United States, liquidate is standard in business, law and finance, as in 'the company will liquidate its assets' or 'the store is liquidating its inventory.' A shop sign that says 'Everything must go' describes the same situation in plain language. In everyday speech, people usually say 'sell off' or 'close out,' and 'liquidate' can sound grim.

distinctions.note: Sell off is informal and general, while liquidate usually means selling all assets to settle debts or close a business.
To dissolve a company is to end its legal existence, while liquidating it is the process of converting its assets into cash.

examples.everyday: My uncle's hardware store closed, and they're liquidating everything at half price this weekend.
examples.professional: Finance wants us to liquidate the legacy positions by Friday to free up cash for the new contracts.
examples.analytical: Bankruptcy law distinguishes between reorganizing a firm and liquidating its assets to satisfy creditors.

nuance.analogy: Liquidating a business is like emptying a warehouse into a truck and turning every item into cash, so the debts can be paid.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin 'liquidare,' to make liquid or clear, from Latin 'liquidus,' liquid.
common_mistakes: Using 'liquidate' to mean 'liquefy' in ordinary speech, which sounds technical.
Forgetting that in business it means selling assets, not just making them liquid.

senses.definition: Using a language model to grade or compare other models' outputs.

core.definition: Using a language model to grade, score, or compare the outputs of other models or systems, instead of relying only on human raters.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on JUDGE, and the phrase words 'as' and 'a' are reduced to 'az' and 'uh'. The word 'EM' gets only a light secondary stress.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a method name in AI evaluation, not an evaluative term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this in machine-learning evaluation, often in a team meeting or a design review. Practitioners usually add that it has known biases, such as preferring longer answers or the first option shown, so they validate it against human labels. A natural reply is 'Sure, but we should check it against human ratings first.'

distinctions.note: Human evaluation is more trusted and expensive, but slower; LLM-as-a-judge is faster and cheaper but needs validation.
A benchmark uses fixed tests with known answers; LLM-as-a-judge can assess open-ended answers that have no single right result.

collocations: use an LLM as a judge

examples.everyday: My colleague wants to use LLM-as-a-judge to rate the chatbot answers, but I'm not sure we can trust it yet.
examples.professional: For the release review, we'll run LLM-as-a-judge on the test set and compare its scores with the human rater sample.
examples.analytical: LLM-as-a-judge assumes that a model's preference correlates with human judgment, an assumption that must be tested rather than taken for granted.

nuance.analogy: It's like having a second teacher grade essays with a rubric: fast and consistent, but you still check a sample against a human grader.
nuance.etymology: A recent coinage in AI evaluation, combining LLM with the phrase as a judge.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'judge' as 'joodge' with a long u; the vowel is short.
Dropping 'as' or 'a' in speech and writing, which makes the expression harder to parse.

conversation.text: LLM-as-a-judge uses a strong model to grade other models' outputs against a rubric.
LLM-as-a-judge setups can favor longer answers or the first response shown, so we randomize the order.
Before trusting LLM-as-a-judge scores, check their agreement with human ratings on a sample.

senses.definition: Dispute over the meaning of words.
A conflict waged only as a battle of words.

core.definition: A dispute fought over the meaning of words, or an argument that consists only of words and has no real substance behind it.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, 'GAH'. The -chy ending is spelled with a 'ch' but is pronounced as a 'k'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies a pointless or hair-splitting quarrel.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in academic, literary, or theological writing and in formal essays, especially to criticize a debate about definitions. It is rare in speech, and in conversation people would say 'arguing over semantics' or 'a war of words' instead. It is a sophisticated choice that signals education.

distinctions.note: Wordplay is playful and often clever, while logomachy is a contentious quarrel about the meaning of words.
Sophistry is deliberately misleading reasoning, while logomachy is a dispute that may be sincere but focused on words.

examples.professional: The design review turned into a logomachy about whether a feature was a 'bug' or a 'limitation', and nothing got decided.
examples.analytical: Much of the medieval dispute over the nature of universals struck later critics as logomachy, a quarrel about terms rather than things.

nuance.analogy: A logomachy is like two people fencing with dictionaries, each cutting at the other's definitions while the actual question goes untouched.
nuance.etymology: From Greek logomachia, 'a battle of words', from logos ('word') and machē ('battle').
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final 'chy' as 'chee', when it sounds like 'kee'.
Using it for any argument; it applies specifically to disputes over words and their meanings.

senses.definition: The property of being lowly.

core.definition: The quality of being humble, modest or of low social rank; a humble attitude toward others.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LOH, the first syllable. The middle syllable is a short 'lee', and the ending is a reduced 'us', not 'ness' with a long e.

nuance.connotation: Positive in religious and moral contexts, where it praises humility. In a social context it can suggest low status and be neutral or sad.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use lowliness mainly in religious writing, literature and formal speech. In everyday talk, they say 'humility' or 'modesty'. Lowliness can sound old-fashioned or preachy if used in casual conversation about yourself.

distinctions.note: Humility is the standard modern word for a modest attitude; lowliness emphasizes low rank or status as well as modesty.
Modesty usually concerns how someone presents themselves; lowliness can describe a whole condition of life.

examples.everyday: My grandmother never boasted, and people admired her lowliness.
examples.professional: In the leadership seminar, we discussed lowliness as a quality that makes managers easier to trust.
examples.analytical: The author treats lowliness not as weakness but as the moral center of the narrative, a freely chosen posture toward others.

nuance.analogy: Like a house built near the ground: it is sturdy and close to others, not on a tall tower that looks down on them.
nuance.etymology: From lowly (Old English lāg, low) and the suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Using 'lowliness' to mean 'low quality' or 'low price', which is not its meaning.
Using it in everyday small talk where 'humble' or 'modest' sounds more natural.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word behind lowliness is tapeinophrosynē (ταπεινοφροσύνη), 'humility, lowliness of mind', from tapeinos (low, humble). Philippians 2:3 urges believers, in humility, to count others better than themselves. Luke 1:48 records Mary's words about God regarding the lowly condition of his servant. Micah 6:8 summarizes what the Lord requires as doing justice and walking humbly with God.

senses.definition: Initialism of long short-term memory.

core.definition: Long short-term memory: a type of recurrent neural network that learns patterns across long sequences, such as text or time series.

pronunciation.tip: Say the letters one by one: 'el', 'ess', 'tee', then 'EM' with the main stress. Don't say it as one word like 'LIST-em'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical; it is a precise term in machine learning.
nuance.usage_note: Data scientists and machine learning engineers say LSTM in meetings, papers and code. Teams may also say 'the LSTM model' or 'an LSTM layer'. For non-experts, it is fine to say 'a recurrent neural network' and give the full name the first time. Americans spell out the letters rather than saying 'lstm' as a word.

distinctions.note: An RNN is the general category of recurrent network; an LSTM is a specific RNN design with gates that help it remember information over long gaps.
A GRU is a simpler gated recurrent unit with fewer gates; an LSTM has separate forget, input and output gates.

examples.everyday: My coworker says the LSTM model we built last year is still running in production.
examples.professional: In today's meeting, let's compare the LSTM baseline with the transformer model on the forecasting task.
examples.analytical: The LSTM's gating mechanism addresses the vanishing gradient problem by controlling what information persists across time steps.

nuance.analogy: Like a notebook with a few sticky notes: it remembers important things over time and decides what to keep or erase.
nuance.etymology: Named for long short-term memory, the design introduced by Sepp Hochreiter and Jürgen Schmidhuber in 1997.
common_mistakes: Saying 'L-S-T-M' as one word, 'lis-tem', rather than spelling the letters.
Confusing LSTM with a general neural network; it is a specific type of recurrent network.

conversation.text: An LSTM can carry information across long sequences better than a plain RNN.
The LSTM baseline is still competitive on our short time series.
The LSTM's cell state acts like a conveyor belt that gates can add to or erase from.

senses.definition: A fretted stringed instrument, similar to the guitar, having a bowl-shaped body or soundbox; any of a wide variety of chordophones with a pear-shaped body and a neck whose upper surface is in the same plane as the soundboard, with strings along the neck and parallel to the soundboard.
Thick sticky clay or cement used to close up a hole or gap, especially to make something air-tight.
A packing ring, as of rubber, for fruit jars, etc.
A straight-edged piece of wood for striking off superfluous clay from earth.
To play on a lute, or as if on a lute.
To fix or fasten something with lute.

core.definition: A stringed musical instrument with a pear-shaped body and a fretted neck, plucked with the fingers, popular in medieval and Renaissance music.

pronunciation.tip: This is a single syllable pronounced like 'loot', with a long oo sound and a final t that is released clearly. It is not 'loot' with a flapped t.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It refers to a historical instrument and is mostly used in music, history and literature.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use lute mainly for the historical plucked instrument in music classes, concerts and museums. In everyday conversation it is uncommon, and people might say guitar or mandolin for a similar modern instrument. The word also appears in biblical translations, where it can be a translation of the Hebrew word for a harp or lyre.
word_family: luthier (noun, related maker of stringed instruments)

distinctions.note: A guitar is a modern instrument with a flat body and frets, while a lute has a rounded, pear-shaped back and was used in older European music.
A lyre is an ancient harp-like instrument with a U-shaped frame, while a lute has a neck and a rounded body.

examples.everyday: At the museum, the docent showed us a lute from the sixteenth century.
examples.professional: Our orchestra is adding a lute part to the Renaissance program next season.
examples.analytical: The lute's place in medieval court music shows how instruments carried social and cultural meaning.

nuance.analogy: A lute is like an old ancestor of the guitar, with a rounded body that feels like a pear.
nuance.etymology: From Old French lut, from Old Provençal laut, from Arabic al-'ud, meaning the wood.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like 'lewt' with a long u that sounds like 'lyoot'; the American vowel is simply 'loot'.
Confusing lute with lyre or harp, which are different instruments.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Hebrew Bible the word usually behind lute is nebel, an instrument of uncertain shape that the RSV often renders as harp or lyre. The RSV keeps lute in some places. Psalm 33:2 calls for praise with the lyre and the harp of ten strings. Psalm 150:3 calls for praise with trumpet, lute and harp, showing the instrument used in temple worship.

lute.etymology: From Middle French *lut* (modern *luth*), from Old French *leut*, probably from Old Occitan *laüt*, from Arabic *عود* (“wood”).

senses.definition: Faulty functioning.
Failure to function.
To function improperly.
senses.example: She told him the machine was poorly built, but they both knew that she was the one who had malfunctioned.

senses.definition: To fail to function.

core.definition: A failure to work or operate correctly, especially in a machine, device, or system.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on FUNK, with a lighter secondary stress on mal-. Say 'shun' as a single reduced syllable, not 'shee-ahn'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It describes a problem in equipment or systems and usually implies a need for repair.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use malfunction constantly for machines, software, medical devices, and systems, such as 'the alarm had a malfunction.' In casual speech people often say 'it's broken' or 'it's acting up.' Used for people, it sounds odd or medical.

distinctions.note: A breakdown is a complete stop, often of a vehicle or a mental or social system. A malfunction can be partial and may still allow limited operation.
Glitch is informal and usually refers to a small temporary problem in software. Malfunction sounds more formal and can describe serious equipment failure.

examples.everyday: Our dishwasher had a malfunction again, so we called the repair guy.
examples.professional: The deployment failed because of a malfunction in the load balancer, so we rolled back the release.
examples.analytical: Philosophers of technology ask whether a malfunction is defined by the designer's intention or by the machine's actual performance.

nuance.analogy: A malfunction is like a car that suddenly stops running in the middle of traffic: it was built to work, and something inside failed.
nuance.etymology: From mal- 'bad' combined with function, from Latin functio, 'performance.'
common_mistakes: Using it as a verb with an object, as in 'the device malfunctioned the printer'; the verb is intransitive, so say 'the printer malfunctioned.'
Stressing the second syllable, saying 'mal-FUNK-shun' correctly but dropping the stress on 'mal' in careful speech.

senses.definition: A person whose job is to manage something, such as a business, a restaurant, or a sports team.
A window or application whose purpose is to give the user the control over some aspect of the system.
senses.example: a file manager; a task manager; Program Manager

senses.definition: The head coach.
An administrator, for a singer or group. (Can we add an example for this sense?)

core.definition: A person paid to run or supervise a business, store, restaurant, team, department or other group.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle vowel is a quick ih, and the final -er is a reduced r sound, not a separate syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most contexts; positive when praising someone as a good manager.
nuance.usage_note: This is the everyday word for a supervisor or head of a business unit. Americans say 'Can I speak to the manager?' in stores and restaurants, usually politely. For sports, manager means the head coach in baseball, while basketball and football normally use coach.

distinctions.note: Boss is more informal and direct, while manager is the standard job title.
A supervisor usually oversees daily work at a lower level, while a manager often has wider authority over a group or budget.
A director is usually a senior leader over several managers, often in a larger organization.

examples.everyday: I asked the restaurant manager if they could seat us by the window.
examples.professional: My manager wants the dashboard ready before Thursday's review.
examples.analytical: A manager's authority depends less on rank than on the ability to coordinate people toward shared goals.

nuance.analogy: A manager is like an orchestra conductor: the musicians play, but the conductor keeps them together.
nuance.etymology: From manage, from Italian maneggiare 'to handle, train horses,' plus the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle syllable with a full vowel, as in mana-JAY.
Using manager only as an insult; it is a job title, while boss is the informal word for the person in charge.

conversation.text: The cashier said she needed a manager to approve the return.
Can I speak to the manager? I've been waiting for twenty minutes.
The store manager gave us a discount because the item was damaged.

core.definition: The mother of Jesus in the New Testament, a young Jewish woman of Nazareth honored in Christian tradition.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, which rhymes with 'air', not 'mar'. Avoid pronouncing it like 'Marie' or 'Mah-ree'.

nuance.connotation: Reverent in religious contexts; neutral as a common name.
nuance.usage_note: Mary is among the most common American given names, as well as the name of the mother of Jesus. In religious talk, specify which Mary if needed. Catholics and Orthodox often say 'the Virgin Mary', 'Mother of God', or 'the Blessed Virgin'.

distinctions.note: Mary Magdalene was a different woman, a follower of Jesus from Magdala.
Miriam is the Hebrew form of the name, including Moses' sister, and is the source of 'Mary'.

examples.everyday: At our church's Christmas play, my daughter was Mary and my nephew was Joseph.
examples.professional: This week's lesson looks at how Luke portrays Mary's response to the angel's announcement.
examples.analytical: Marian doctrine shows how a figure who speaks little in Scripture could become central to debates about Christ's nature.

nuance.etymology: From Greek Maria/Mariam, from Hebrew Miriam, of uncertain meaning.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like 'mah-ree' or 'MAR-ee' with an 'ar' vowel.
Confusing Mary with Mary Magdalene.
nuance.biblical_note: Greek Maria or Mariam, from Hebrew Miriam. Luke 1:26-38 tells of the angel announcing that she will bear Jesus. Luke 1:46-55 records her song of praise, the Magnificat. John 19:25-27 shows her at the cross, where Jesus entrusts her to the beloved disciple.

traditions.view: Mary is honored as Mother of God, taught to be immaculately conceived, ever-virgin, and assumed into heaven; Catholics ask for her intercession.
Mary is the Theotokos ('God-bearer') and ever-virgin, highly venerated, and her dormition is celebrated; Orthodox do not define the Immaculate Conception as Catholics do.

Protestants honor Mary as the mother of Jesus and a model of faith, but generally reject praying to her and Marian dogmas beyond Scripture. Lutherans and Anglicans keep more reverence for her, and some of them, following Luther and the early Reformers, hold her perpetual virginity; many Baptists and Pentecostals see her simply as a faithful servant.

core.definition: A Hebrew personal name borne by several men in the Old Testament, including the original name of King Zedekiah of Judah.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on NY, the middle syllable of the name. Keep the final vowel short and reduced to uh rather than saying a full ee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a name used in Scripture and Bible study.
nuance.usage_note: Americans would use this name only in Bible study, scholarship, or church settings, and rarely in ordinary conversation. Mentioning it usually leads to a discussion of Zedekiah or Nehemiah's Levites. Say Zedekiah when you mean the king in everyday talk.

distinctions.note: Mattithiah is a different Hebrew name, spelled and stressed similarly, and borne by different Levites and temple figures.
Zedekiah is the name the king received after Nebuchadnezzar placed him on the throne, replacing Mattaniah.

examples.everyday: Did you know the last king of Judah was originally named Mattaniah before the Babylonians changed his name?
examples.professional: In the lesson plan, I list Mattaniah and point out that his renaming shows Babylonian control over Judah.
examples.analytical: The renaming of Mattaniah as Zedekiah signals a political act of vassalage, marking his allegiance to Nebuchadnezzar.

nuance.analogy: Like a person who gets a new title when someone else takes control of their country, Mattaniah becomes Zedekiah when Babylon names him king.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Mattanyah, meaning gift of Yahweh.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in MAT-uh-NY-uh, which is not the natural American pattern.
Confusing Mattaniah with Mattithiah, whose stress and sound pattern differ slightly.
Using Mattaniah as a common English word when speaking of the king; the usual name is Zedekiah.
nuance.biblical_note: Mattaniah (Hebrew Mattanyah, gift of Yahweh) is the original name of King Zedekiah of Judah. 2 Kings 24:17 says Nebuchadnezzar placed him on the throne and changed his name to Zedekiah. 1 Chronicles 9:15 names a Levite called Mattaniah. Nehemiah 11:17 names a Levite Mattaniah, a leader who led thanksgiving.

senses.definition: A manual worker; a laborer or artisan.
Someone who builds or repairs machinery, a technician; now specifically, someone who works with and repairs the mechanical parts of a motor vehicle, aircraft or similar.
A device, method or means; a function.
senses.example: This game has a mechanic where if you run toward a ledge you automatically jump off rather than just falling.

senses.definition: A function, rule or other implementation that dictates gameplay; a ludeme, a feature.
senses.example: This game has a mechanic where if you run toward a ledge you automatically jump off rather than just falling.

senses.definition: A hitman.
A cheat who manipulates the cards or dice.

core.definition: A person trained to repair and maintain cars, trucks, or other machines with moving mechanical parts.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, KAN. The first syllable is a weak 'muh,' and the final -ic is a short 'ik,' not 'eek.' Do not say 'MEK-uh-nik' with stress on the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. Mechanics are respected for their skill, though people may worry about being overcharged.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'my mechanic' or 'the mechanic' for the person who fixes a car, and they usually mean an auto mechanic. You can say 'I need to take my car to the mechanic' in a casual conversation with a neighbor. A typical reply is 'What's wrong with it?' or 'Do you know a good one?'

distinctions.note: A technician is a broader, more technical term for someone who maintains equipment, often in labs or electronics; a mechanic usually works on vehicles or heavy machines.
A mechanical engineer designs machines and systems; a mechanic builds, repairs, or maintains them.

examples.everyday: My car is making a grinding noise, so I'm taking it to the mechanic on Saturday.
examples.professional: Our fleet manager uses a certified mechanic for every service so the repair records stay consistent.
examples.analytical: The word mechanic has shifted from a general term for a skilled artisan to a specific term for someone who repairs motor vehicles.

nuance.analogy: A mechanic is like a doctor for machines: they diagnose what is wrong and fix the parts that have failed.
nuance.etymology: From Greek mēkhanikos, of machines, from mēkhanē, machine.
common_mistakes: Using 'mechanic' for a mechanical engineer, who designs machines rather than repairs them.
Stressing the first syllable, as in 'MEK-uh-nik.'

mechanic.etymology: From Middle English *mekanyk* (“mechanical”), from Old French *mecanique*, from Latin *mechanicus* (“of or belonging to machines or mechanics, inventive”), from Ancient Greek *μηχανικός* (“pertaining to machines or contrivance, mechanic, ingenious,…

conversation.text: My mechanic said the brakes have another few months left.
Do you know a good mechanic who won't rip me off?
The mechanic called to say the part won't arrive until Thursday.

senses.definition: The act of persons or things that meet.
senses.example: Meeting him will be exciting. I enjoy meeting new people.

senses.definition: A gathering of persons for a purpose; an assembly.
senses.example: We need to have a meeting about that soon.

senses.definition: The people at such a gathering.
senses.example: What has the meeting decided.

senses.definition: An encounter between people, even accidental.
senses.example: They came together in a chance meeting on the way home from work.

senses.definition: A place or instance of junction or intersection; a confluence.
senses.example: Earthquakes occur at the meeting of tectonic plates.

senses.definition: An administrative unit in the Religious Society of Friends (Quakers).
senses.example: Denver meeting is a part of Intermountain yearly meeting.

senses.definition: A religious service held by a charismatic preacher in small towns in the United States.

core.definition: A gathering of people, often at work or in an organization, to discuss or decide something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MEE. The second syllable is a quick, reduced ih sound, and the final ng is clear, with no hard g after it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a standard word for workplace or organizational gatherings, and it can sound tiresome if there are too many.
nuance.usage_note: In American workplaces, meeting is the everyday word for any scheduled discussion, whether a quick check-in or a long planning session. People say I have a meeting at two, or Can we set up a meeting? Calling it a meet or a gathering would sound odd in business, though meet is used for sporting events.
word_family: meet (noun, as in a track meet)

distinctions.note: Conference usually means a larger event with presentations, while meeting is a smaller gathering for discussion.
Appointment is a set time with a person or service, such as a doctor, while meeting is usually a group or work discussion.

examples.everyday: Sorry I'm late, my boss's meeting ran over.
examples.professional: Let's schedule a meeting for Monday morning to review the quarterly results.
examples.analytical: A meeting in organizational theory is not merely a gathering but a ritual that allocates authority and constructs shared meaning among participants.

nuance.analogy: A meeting is like a crossroads where several roads of information come together and then branch out again.
nuance.etymology: From Old English mētan, to meet, with the -ing suffix forming a noun.
common_mistakes: Saying I have a meeting with you in the sense of a casual chat, when Americans often say I'll see you, or we're meeting.
Using meeting with an article in a general sense, for example I like meeting, where the sense is usually plural or with a specific reference.

meeting.etymology: From Middle English *meeting*, *meting*, from Old English *mēting*, *ġemēting* (“meeting, assembly, association, society”), equivalent to *meet* + *-ing*.

conversation.text: I'm in back-to-back meetings until two, but I can call you after that.
Can we set up a quick meeting with the client to go over the numbers?
Honestly, that meeting could have been an email.

senses.definition: A holy candelabrum with seven branches used in the Temple of Jerusalem.
A candelabrum with nine branches, used in Jewish worship on Hanukkah.

core.definition: A candelabrum with branches for lights, used in Jewish worship. Most Americans mean the nine-branched Hanukkah lamp.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on NOR. The first and last vowels are reduced, and the r is pronounced clearly in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and respectful. It refers to a religious symbol and should be used respectfully.
nuance.usage_note: Americans commonly say 'menorah' for the Hanukkah lamp in homes, schools, and public displays in December, even though the traditional Temple lamp had seven branches. A nine-branched lamp is technically a hanukkiah, but many people use 'menorah' for both. Use it respectfully and avoid joking about it.

distinctions.note: A hanukkiah is the nine-branched Hanukkah lamp. Menorah most precisely refers to the seven-branched Temple lampstand, though Americans often use it for both.
Candelabrum is the general term for any branched candle holder. Menorah is a specific Jewish religious object.

collocations: place the menorah in the window

examples.everyday: We put the menorah in our front window every December during Hanukkah.
examples.professional: The office holiday display included a menorah next to the Christmas tree.
examples.analytical: The seven-branched menorah in the Temple became a central symbol of Jewish identity and worship.

nuance.analogy: A menorah is like a lighthouse of ancient faith, with each flame marking a path back to the Temple.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew menorah, lampstand, from a root meaning to shine or light.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, such as ME-nor-ah. The stress is on NOR.
Assuming a menorah always has seven branches. Hanukkah lamps usually have nine.
nuance.biblical_note: The menorah is the golden lampstand of the Tabernacle and Temple, described in Hebrew as menorah, lampstand. Key passages: Exodus 25:31-40 gives the design of the golden lampstand with seven lamps; Numbers 8:1-4 describes Aaron setting up the lamps so that they give light before the lampstand; Exodus 37:17-24 repeats the description of its craftsmanship.

senses.definition: Filled with miasma; containing noxious vapors.
Composed of or resembling vapors.

core.definition: Filled with miasma, meaning foul or poisonous vapors that were once thought to cause disease, or resembling such vapors.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, -AZ-, and the first vowel is a diphthong like 'my'. Learners often stress the first syllable or say 'mee-AZ-mik' by analogy with 'miasma'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. The word describes something foul, heavy or unhealthy, whether a literal vapor or a gloomy atmosphere.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mostly in writing, especially literary criticism, descriptive prose and some science history. In conversation it sounds bookish, so most people would say 'foul-smelling' or 'gloomy' instead. The figurative sense, an oppressive mood or atmosphere, is more common than the literal one.

distinctions.note: 'Noxious' is a general word for harmful or poisonous; 'miasmic' specifically suggests a heavy, foul vapor or a murky atmosphere.
'Stifling' describes air or a place that is hard to breathe in; 'miasmic' adds the sense of something corrupt or unhealthy hanging in the air.

examples.everyday: After the storm, the whole basement smelled damp and miasmic, so we opened every window.
examples.professional: The old server room had a miasmic smell of burnt dust, and facilities had to clean it before anyone could work there.
examples.analytical: Dickens often renders the London fog as a miasmic presence that corrupts both body and conscience.

nuance.analogy: A miasmic place is like a room where the air has gone stale and heavy, so you feel the air itself is sick.
nuance.etymology: From Greek miasma, pollution or stain, from miainein, to stain or defile.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in 'MY-az-mik'.
Using 'miasmic' for any bad smell in everyday speech, where 'smelly' or 'musty' is more natural.

senses.definition: Pertaining to the belief in an impending period of one thousand years of peace and righteousness associated with the Second Coming of Christ and his reign on earth.
Pertaining to any of various religious or social movements which believe in a coming or ongoing radical change to existing world order.
Lasting or expected to last a thousand years.
A person who believes in an apocalyptic millennium.

core.definition: Relating to the belief in a coming thousand-year age of peace under Christ, or in a coming radical transformation of the world.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on 'NAIR', with secondary stress on the first syllable. Americans say the r clearly, and the ending is 'ee-un', not 'ee-ARE-ee-un'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in scholarship; can sound mildly negative or dismissive when describing extreme movements.
nuance.usage_note: Used mainly by historians, sociologists, and theologians to describe movements expecting a dramatic end or renewal of the world. Everyday Americans rarely use it. It is broader than 'millennialist' because it can cover secular movements as well.

distinctions.note: Millennial usually refers to the generation born roughly 1981-1996, or less often to the thousand-year period itself.
Apocalyptic stresses a catastrophic end or revelation, while millenarian stresses an expected age of renewal.
Chiliast is a rarer, technical word for a believer in a literal thousand-year reign.

examples.everyday: My history professor says the group was millenarian, always sure the world was about to change.
examples.professional: The report examines millenarian rhetoric in online communities and how it drives recruitment.
examples.analytical: Medieval millenarian movements often combined social grievance with the hope of an imminent, divinely wrought reversal of power.

nuance.analogy: A millenarian is someone who lives as if dawn is about to break on a completely new world.
nuance.etymology: From Latin millenarius, 'containing a thousand', from mille, 'thousand'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'millennial' (the generation).
Stressing the wrong syllable, as 'mil-LEN-uh-ree-un'.
Spelling it with one n, as 'milenarian'.
nuance.biblical_note: The idea rests chiefly on Revelation 20:1-6, which speaks of a thousand-year reign of Christ and the saints. Interpreters disagree about whether this is literal or symbolic. Isaiah 11:6-9 is often cited as a picture of the peace expected.

senses.definition: To make (something) smaller or as small as possible; shrink; reduce.
senses.example: We have to minimize the budget.

senses.definition: To relegate or assign (something) to a less insignificant status; diminish.
senses.example: The insurance adjuster tried to minimize the extent of the damage to lessen the company's exposure to liability.

senses.definition: To remove (a window) from the main display area, collapsing it to an icon or caption.
senses.example: I didn't close anything, but I minimized all the windows so I could see the desktop.

senses.definition: To treat (someone) in a slighting manner.
To treat as trivial or insignificant; to trivialize.
senses.example: to minimize someone's feelings

core.definition: To reduce something to the smallest amount or degree possible, or to make it seem less important than it is.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle syllable is short, and the final -ize sounds like "eyes." Do not say "min-ih-MY-zuh."

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative when used to downplay problems, as in "minimize the damage."
nuance.usage_note: Americans use minimize both for reducing physical or quantitative things, as in "minimize risk," and for downplaying problems, as in "don't minimize the issue." In meetings it is common and professional. The spelling is minimize in American English; minimise is British.

distinctions.note: Reduce is the general word for making something smaller; minimize means making it as small as possible or treating it as small.
Downplay means to present something as less important; minimize can refer to actual reduction in size or quantity as well.

examples.everyday: I'm trying to minimize my screen time before bed, so I put my phone in the other room.
examples.professional: We need to minimize downtime during the migration, so let's schedule it for Saturday night.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that the author minimizes the role of institutions in shaping moral choice.

nuance.analogy: Minimizing is like folding a map until it fits in your pocket: the same content, but as small as it can get.
nuance.etymology: From Latin minimus (smallest), plus the verb suffix -ize.
common_mistakes: Spelling it minimise, the British form, in American writing.
Using minimize with a preposition, as in "minimize on the costs"; use it without "on."
patterns: minimize f(x) over/with respect to x

senses.definition: To change part of.
senses.example: Her publisher advised her to modify a few parts of the book to make it easier to read.

senses.definition: To be or become modified.
To set bounds to; to moderate.
To qualify the meaning of.

core.definition: To change something somewhat, usually to make it better fit a need, or to make a small adjustment without changing its basic nature.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MAH. The middle syllable is a reduced, quick ih. The final syllable rhymes with my or fly, so the word ends with a clear -fy sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes adjustment rather than improvement or damage.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use modify in technical, legal, and business talk, as in modify the settings or modify the agreement. In casual speech people more often say change or adjust. In grammar, a word modifies another word when it describes or limits it.

distinctions.note: Change is the general and everyday word; modify suggests a more careful, partial adjustment that leaves the core unchanged.
Adjust usually means to fine-tune something to fit; modify can mean a broader change to its form or content.

examples.everyday: Can you modify the recipe a little so it's not so spicy for the kids?
examples.professional: We need to modify the API so the new service can accept the older data format without breaking the app.
examples.analytical: Kant does not simply reject the empirical; he modifies our understanding of how experience is structured by the mind.

nuance.analogy: To modify something is like turning the dial on a radio: you adjust the signal so it comes through more clearly, but it is still the same station.
nuance.etymology: From Latin modificare, from modus meaning measure and facere meaning to make.
common_mistakes: Using modify with a preposition, as in modify to; the verb takes a direct object.
Confusing modify with magnify or modernize; each has a different meaning.

modify.etymology: From Middle English *modifien*, from Middle French *modifier*, from Latin *modificare* (“to limit, control, regulate, deponent”), from *modificari* (“to measure off, set bound to, moderate”), from *modus* (“measure”) + *facere* (“to make”); see *mode*.

core.definition: A town in ancient Judea, the hometown and family burial place of Mattathias and his sons, the Maccabees, who led the revolt against Antiochus IV.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MOH. Keep the vowel in the second syllable short and unstressed, so the name sounds like MOH-din rather than moh-DEEN.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a place name with historical and religious associations.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly meet this name in Bible study, Jewish history, or discussions of the Maccabean revolt. Readers of 1 Maccabees may see it spelled Modein in some editions. In everyday speech it rarely comes up, so it is safest to name the context when you mention it.

examples.everyday: My Bible study group read about Mattathias last week, and the leader said his family came from a village called Modin.
examples.professional: For the history lecture, include a slide showing where Modin sits relative to Jerusalem and the Hasmonean territories.
examples.analytical: The author places the family's origin at Modin, which gives the revolt a rural base rather than a Jerusalem-centered one.

nuance.analogy: Modin is like a small hometown that becomes famous because a famous family started there and was buried there.
nuance.etymology: Hebrew Modi'in, the name of a village in ancient Judea.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in moh-DEEN, which is not the usual American pattern.
Confusing Modin with Jerusalem or other Maccabean sites; Modin was a village, not the capital.
nuance.biblical_note: Modin is not in the Protestant canon but appears in 1 Maccabees, which Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include and which the RSV Apocrypha contains. It was the home village of the priest Mattathias, who started the revolt against Antiochus IV around 167 B.C. 1 Maccabees 2:1 introduces Mattathias as a priest living at Modein. 1 Maccabees 2:70 says he was buried in the tombs of his fathers at Modein. 1 Maccabees 13:25-30 describes Simon burying his father and brothers there and building a monument.

senses.definition: A tiny amount.
The smallest particle of a specific element or compound that retains the chemical properties of that element or compound; two or more atoms held together by chemical bonds.
senses.example: Hydrogen chloride is a diatomic molecule, consisting of a hydrogen atom and a chlorine atom.

core.definition: The smallest unit of a chemical compound or element that keeps its chemical properties, made of two or more atoms bonded together.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle syllable is weak, like "lih." Pronounce the last syllable as "kyool," with a clear "y" sound before the "oo."

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise scientific term, but Americans also use it casually for a tiny bit of something.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use "molecule" in chemistry, biology, and everyday science talk. In casual speech, people sometimes say "a molecule of" to mean a tiny amount, as in "not a molecule of doubt." For general discussion of tiny things, people may say "particle" instead.

distinctions.note: An atom is the smallest unit of an element. A molecule is formed when two or more atoms are chemically bonded.
"Particle" is a general term for a small piece of matter. "Molecule" is a precise chemical term.

examples.everyday: Not a molecule of that cake is left, so we're going to have to bake another one.
examples.professional: The sensor detects individual molecules of the gas, so we can measure concentrations down to very low levels.
examples.analytical: A molecule's three-dimensional shape determines how it binds to a receptor, which is why small structural changes can matter so much.

nuance.analogy: A molecule is like a LEGO structure made of several bricks snapped together: each piece is an atom, and the whole is the molecule.
nuance.etymology: From French "molécule," from Latin "moleculum," a diminutive of "moles," meaning mass.
common_mistakes: Using "molecule" for any tiny piece of matter, when "particle" or "atom" might be more accurate.
Stressing the second syllable, as in "muh-LEK-yool," which is not the American pattern.

senses.definition: An ultimate atom, or simple, unextended point; something ultimate and indivisible.
One thing, one being, one item.
A group of entities or items treated as one entity.
A single-celled organism. (See Monas.)
A monoid object in the category of endofunctors of a fixed category.
A data type which represents a specific form of computation, along with the operations "return" and "bind".
A single individual (such as a pollen grain) that is free from others, not united in a group.

core.definition: In philosophy, an indivisible, simple unit of being that has no parts and is the basic building block of reality.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MOH. The final syllable rhymes with 'bad' and ends with a clear d.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use monad mainly in philosophy, theology, and mathematics. In philosophy classes it usually refers to Leibniz's idea of simple substances. Outside academic settings, most people would not recognize the word, so it is best used with clear explanation.

distinctions.note: An atom in modern science is physically divisible, while a philosophical monad is a simple, non-physical unit that has no parts at all.
Unit is a general word for one item or measure, while monad specifically means a simple, indivisible substance in metaphysics.

examples.everyday: In my philosophy class, the professor said a monad is a kind of basic unit of being, not an atom.
examples.professional: The speaker at the seminar used monad to describe an indivisible unit of computation in her model.
examples.analytical: Leibniz argues that every monad mirrors the whole universe from its own particular point of view.

nuance.analogy: A monad is like a tiny mirror that reflects the whole universe from one point, with no separate pieces inside it.
