nuance.etymology: From Late Latin monas, from Greek monas 'unit', from monos 'alone'.
common_mistakes: Using monad as a general word for any unit or group.
Confusing it with monk, which is pronounced differently and has a different meaning.
Assuming the philosophical sense is physical, like an atom.

monad.etymology: From Latin *monas* (“unit”) (from Ancient Greek *μονάς*, from *μόνος*, from Proto-Indo-European **men-*).

senses.definition: A set which is closed under an associative binary operation, and which contains an element which is an identity for the operation.
Containing only one kind of metrical foot.

core.definition: A set with an associative operation and an identity element, such as the natural numbers under addition with zero.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the second vowel is a clear OY diphthong. Do not pronounce the final d as a separate syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: it is a precise term in mathematics.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use monoid in algebra, theoretical computer science and functional programming. It appears in graduate courses and technical papers. Students usually learn it after groups, which are monoids with inverses.

distinctions.note: A group is a monoid where every element has an inverse; a monoid need not have inverses.
A semigroup has an associative operation but no required identity element; a monoid requires one.

examples.everyday: My son is studying algebra and asked me what a monoid is, so I said it is like a group without the inverses.
examples.professional: The parser can be modeled as a monoid, so combining partial results is associative and easy to parallelize.
examples.analytical: A monoid is defined by an associative binary operation together with an identity element, and the structure captures concatenation of strings.

nuance.analogy: Like adding numbers with zero, a monoid combines things in a grouped way and always has a do-nothing element.
common_mistakes: Confusing monoid with monad, which is a related but different concept in category theory and programming.
Assuming a monoid has inverses; that is a group.

core.definition: A Christian title for Mary, mother of Jesus, affirming that her son is truly God as well as man.

pronunciation.tip: Say 'MUTH-er uv GAHD' with the 'th' voiced as in 'this'. 'God' has the open 'ah' vowel, not 'gawd' in the Northeast, and 'of' reduces to 'uv'.

nuance.connotation: Reverent and positive in Catholic and Orthodox use; may be controversial or misunderstood by some Protestants.
nuance.usage_note: Americans hear this title in Catholic and Orthodox churches and in prayers like the Hail Mary ('Holy Mary, Mother of God'). Used outside the faith, it can sound surprising to some. It is a theological claim about Christ, not a claim that Mary existed before God.

distinctions.note: Theotokos is the Greek form of the title, used in Orthodox liturgy and theology.
Virgin Mary emphasizes her virginity; Mother of God emphasizes who her son is.
Mother of Jesus is the neutral biblical description; Mother of God makes an explicit claim about his divinity.

collocations: pray to the Mother of God
Solemnity of Mary, Mother of God

examples.everyday: My Catholic grandmother prays the Hail Mary every night: 'Holy Mary, Mother of God, pray for us sinners.'
examples.professional: The lecture covers why the Council of Ephesus defended the title Mother of God.
examples.analytical: The title Mother of God is not a claim about Mary's origin but a safeguard of the unity of Christ's person.

nuance.analogy: Like calling a woman the mother of a king: the title refers to who her child is, not to her own rank.
nuance.etymology: English translation of Greek Theotokos and Latin Mater Dei.
common_mistakes: Taking the title to mean Mary created God.
Pronouncing 'of' with a full vowel instead of 'uv'.
Saying 'MOTHER of GOD' with equal stress; the main stress falls on 'God'.
nuance.biblical_note: The exact phrase is not in Scripture. Luke 1:43 has Elizabeth calling Mary 'the mother of my Lord,' where 'Lord' (Greek kyrios) is a divine title. Luke 1:35 says the child will be called holy, the Son of God. John 1:14 says the Word became flesh, the basis for the claim that Mary's son is God incarnate.

traditions.view: Mother of God is a dogmatic title from Ephesus (431), and Catholics honor Mary with prayers like the Hail Mary and a January 1 solemnity.
The title is used with Theotokos and is central to hymns, icons, and liturgy, which honor Mary as the Mother of God.
Most historic Protestants accept the title as a statement that Jesus is God, though some avoid it for fear of exaggerating Mary's role.

mother-of-god.etymology: Latin *Mater Dei* and its descendants in other languages, from the Christian concept of the Trinity whereby Jesus as God the Son is identical to God the Father as the single divinity.

core.definition: A man from Jezreel who refused to sell his ancestral vineyard to King Ahab and was falsely accused and killed by Jezebel's scheme.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final 'th' is voiceless, as in 'math.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: In American Bible study and sermons, Naboth is a name for a faithful person who refuses to give up inheritance. In everyday speech it appears only in religious or literary references.

distinctions.note: Nabal is the foolish husband of Abigail, while Naboth is the faithful Jezreelite killed over a vineyard.

examples.everyday: My grandmother refused to sell her house to a developer and said she would be like Naboth, holding on to what was hers.
examples.professional: In the ethics module, we used Naboth's vineyard to discuss how a powerful person can misuse legal procedure.
examples.analytical: The account of Naboth in 1 Kings 21 exposes the abuse of royal power, since the king's desire for land leads to a false charge and murder.

nuance.analogy: Naboth is like a small landowner whose property is wanted by a powerful neighbor who uses the courts to take it.
nuance.etymology: Hebrew Navot, a personal name whose meaning is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Confusing him with Nabal.
Saying the final 'th' as 'd' or 't.'
nuance.biblical_note: Naboth (Hebrew Navot) of Jezreel owned a vineyard next to the palace of King Ahab. He refuses to give away his ancestral inheritance, as in 1 Kings 21:3. Jezebel arranges false witnesses, and he is stoned. Elijah then pronounces judgment on Ahab and Jezebel in 1 Kings 21:17-24, making Naboth's case a major story about justice and God's law.

core.definition: The name of two figures in the Bible: Aaron's eldest son who died offering strange fire, and a king of Israel.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final syllable has the short a of 'cat,' not a long a.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Nadab is a biblical name used in Bible study, preaching and church history. Americans would say it as a plain proper name, and it is not used as a common word.

distinctions.note: Abihu is Nadab's brother who also died in Leviticus 10, so the two are often mentioned together.

examples.everyday: In the Bible study, someone asked about Nadab, and we looked up the story of Aaron's sons.
examples.professional: In the seminary lecture, I referred to Nadab and Abihu as the example of priests who acted outside God's instructions.
examples.analytical: The account of Nadab in Leviticus 10 raises questions about worship and holiness that interpreters have debated for centuries.

nuance.analogy: Nadab is like a name in a family history whose story teaches a lesson about careless duty.
nuance.etymology: Hebrew Nadav, 'generous' or 'willing.'
common_mistakes: Confusing him with Nabal or Naboth.
Stressing the second syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: Nadab (Hebrew Nadav, 'generous' or 'willing') was the eldest son of Aaron. Leviticus 10:1-2 says he and his brother Abihu offered unauthorized fire before the LORD and died. A later Nadab, son of Jeroboam, reigned over Israel briefly and is named in 1 Kings 15:25-28, where Baasha kills him and takes the throne.

core.definition: A disciple of Jesus from Cana in Galilee, introduced to Jesus by Philip and praised as a man without guile in the Gospel of John.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, THAN. The final -ael is usually reduced to a short yul sound, not the long ay of the spelling.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In Christian contexts the name carries respect as a disciple.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use Nathanael in church, Bible study or Christian writing, where it names the disciple. Many Americans know the name as Nathaniel, the more common English form. Modern English Bibles such as the RSV use Nathanael.

distinctions.note: Nathanael is a New Testament disciple in John, while Nathan is an Old Testament prophet of David's court.

examples.everyday: Nathanael is one of the early followers in John's Gospel, so my Bible study group talks about him a lot.
examples.professional: Teach Nathanael's call in John 1 as an example of honest doubt meeting a personal encounter with Jesus.
examples.analytical: John's portrait of Nathanael, an Israelite in whom there is no guile, frames sincerity as a central virtue of discipleship.

nuance.analogy: Nathanael is like a skeptic who meets the truth in person and becomes its honest witness.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Netanel, meaning 'God has given'.
common_mistakes: Using Nathanael and Nathan interchangeably, although they are different people.
Stressing the final syllable instead of THAN.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew name Netanel means 'God has given'. Nathanael appears as a disciple brought to Jesus by Philip. In John 1:47 Jesus calls him an Israelite in whom there is no guile, and Nathanael later confesses Jesus as Son of God. In John 21:2 he is listed among disciples at the Sea of Tiberias and is identified as from Cana in Galilee. Some scholars link him with Bartholomew, but the Gospels never state this.

senses.definition: A small detail or distinction.
senses.example: We met the new captain while we were taking enemy fire and were unable to observe the niceties of formal introductions.

senses.definition: Subtlety or precision of use; exactness; preciseness.
senses.example: A rocket-propelled grenade doesn't have the nicety of a sniper round, but you must admit its effectiveness.

senses.definition: A delicacy of character or feeling usually from excessive refinement; fastidiousness.
Synonym of social nicety.
Behaving in an unpleasant or spiteful way that is seemingly, or perceived as, pleasant or agreeable.

core.definition: A small, subtle detail or fine distinction, especially one that matters only to people who care about precision.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the final -ty sounds like a short 'tee' with a reduced vowel. Learners often pronounce the middle syllable too strongly, so keep it short and quick.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; the word is precise and usually admiring when used of careful thinking, but can sound fussy when it describes unimportant details.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nicety mostly in careful writing, legal or academic discussion, or polished speech, as in 'the legal niceties' or 'the niceties of the contract.' In casual talk, people say 'details' or 'fine points' instead. The plural 'niceties' is far more common than the singular.

distinctions.note: A detail is any particular fact; a nicety is a fine point that requires careful attention to notice or handle.
Nuance is a subtle difference in meaning or tone; nicety more often refers to exactness of procedure, wording or conduct.

examples.everyday: I don't care about the social niceties at the party, I just want to meet people.
examples.professional: Let's skip the niceties in the contract review and focus on the liability clause.
examples.analytical: The argument depends on niceties of definition that the critics never address.

nuance.analogy: A nicety is like a grain of salt in a recipe: small, easy to miss, but it changes the final taste.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English 'nice,' meaning foolish or precise, from Latin 'nescius,' ignorant.
common_mistakes: Using 'nicety' to mean 'kindness' or 'pleasantry'; in American English it means a fine detail.
Saying the word with the stress on the second syllable.

nicety.etymology: From Middle English *nicetee*, from Old French *niceté* (“simpleness, foolishness”), from *nice* (“simple, foolish”); equivalent to *nice* + *-e-* + *-ty*.

senses.definition: Not falsifiable.

core.definition: Unable to be proven false by any possible observation or experiment, so it is not scientifically testable.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'FAL' in the middle. The -able ending is reduced to 'uh-bul', and the 'fy' sounds like the word 'fire'.

nuance.connotation: Negative in science, where it suggests a claim is not useful; neutral in philosophy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term mainly in philosophy of science, statistics, and debates about pseudoscience. Calling a claim non-falsifiable is a serious criticism in technical discussion.

distinctions.note: Non-falsifiable and unfalsifiable mean the same thing; the first is slightly more common in writing.
Untestable may mean hard to test in practice; non-falsifiable means no possible test could refute the claim.

examples.everyday: My uncle's theory about the moon landing is so non-falsifiable that no evidence will ever change his mind.
examples.professional: Before we ship the model, we need to make sure our success criterion is not non-falsifiable.
examples.analytical: A hypothesis that forbids no possible observation is non-falsifiable, and Popper would deny it the status of science.

nuance.analogy: A non-falsifiable claim is like a weather forecast that says 'it might rain or might not': nothing could prove it wrong.
nuance.etymology: From non- 'not' and falsifiable, from Latin falsus 'false'.
common_mistakes: Writing 'non-falsificable' with a 'c' instead of the 'f-i-a-b-l-e' spelling.
Stressing the last syllable instead of the 'FAL' syllable.

senses.definition: The state of being new or novel; newness.
A new product; an innovation.
A small mass-produced trinket.
In novelty theory, newness, density of complexification, and dynamic change as opposed to static habituation.
An opening move played for the first time ever (in high-level chess).
In the design of a common household item, often impractically large, and meant primarily for display rather than functional use.
senses.example: My novelty calculator works fine but it hurts my hands to press the keys.

core.definition: The quality of being new, unusual, or different; also a new product or a cheap, small, fun item.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, NAH. The middle syllable reduces to a short 'vul,' and the final 'ty' sounds like 'tee' with a soft t, so it is not 'no-VEL-tee.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative. It can praise freshness, but it often suggests something that is interesting for a short time and not very important.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use novelty for the feeling of something being new and exciting, as in 'the novelty wore off.' They also use novelty item or novelty gift for cheap, fun products sold in gift shops. In store signs and product talk, novelty often means a gimmicky or joke product, so context matters. The adjective novelty-size is used for oversized items meant for display.

distinctions.note: Innovation is a deliberate, useful improvement; novelty is simply the quality of being new, even if it has no lasting value.
Newness is neutral and general; novelty often suggests something interesting or fun that appeals for a short time.

examples.everyday: The novelty of the new coffee machine wore off after a week, and now it just sits on the counter.
examples.professional: The novelty of the feature drew attention, but adoption dropped once users found it did not solve their problem.
examples.analytical: Kant distrusts novelty for its own sake, since the mind is drawn to the strange without necessarily grasping the true.

nuance.analogy: Novelty is like a new toy: exciting at first, but the thrill fades once you know how it works.
nuance.etymology: From Old French novelte, from Latin novellus, 'new.'
common_mistakes: Using novelty as a verb, which it is not; say 'the novelty wore off,' not 'it novelties.'
Confusing novelty with innovation; innovation implies a useful improvement, while novelty may be just new or fun.

novelty.etymology: From Middle English *novelte*, from Old French *novelté* (Modern French *nouveauté*), from the adjective *novel*, ultimately from Latin *novellus*.

senses.definition: A recitation of prayers and devotions for nine consecutive days, especially one to a saint to ask for their intercession.

core.definition: A Catholic devotion of prayers said over nine consecutive days, often to ask for a special intention or a saint's intercession.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on 'VEE'. The final 'a' is a reduced schwa, not 'ah'.

nuance.connotation: Positive and devotional among Catholics; neutral otherwise.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'pray a novena' or 'make a novena'. Familiar in Catholic communities, not widely known outside. A common one is to St. Jude.

distinctions.note: The rosary is a set of prayers counted on beads, usually said in one sitting, while a novena lasts nine days.
A vigil is prayerful watching, usually on one night.
A triduum lasts three days.

examples.everyday: My grandmother started a novena to St. Anthony when she lost her ring.
examples.professional: The parish office is hosting a novena for the feast day, with evening prayers each night.
examples.analytical: The novena's nine-day structure recalls the apostles' prayer between the Ascension and Pentecost.

nuance.analogy: A nine-day knock on heaven's door.
nuance.etymology: From Latin novenus, 'nine each', from novem 'nine'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable.
Saying 'nova-na' with a strong final vowel.
nuance.biblical_note: Acts 1:12-14 describes the apostles praying together with Mary after the Ascension, often cited as the model for nine days of prayer before Pentecost, though the Bible does not name a novena.

traditions.view: Novenas are approved devotions, often seeking the intercession of saints, and Catholics see them as rooted in the nine days before Pentecost.
The novena is not a traditional Orthodox practice, though Orthodox ask saints' intercessions in other prayer services.
Most Protestants do not practice novenas, objecting to prayers to saints, though some Anglicans keep devotions like the Pentecost novena.

senses.definition: Barmy: eccentric, odd; crazy, mad, insane.
senses.example: That student's parents seem to be nutty as a fruitcake.

senses.definition: Containing nuts.
senses.example: This is a nutty chocolate bar.

senses.definition: Resembling or characteristic of nuts.
Extremely attractive, so attractive that one could "nut" (ejaculate) easily or quickly, hot, sexy.

core.definition: Informal: crazy, eccentric, or odd in a silly or unusual way. It can also describe food that contains nuts or tastes like nuts.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and keep the vowel short like the 'u' in 'cup'. The final 'y' is pronounced as 'ee', not 'i' as in 'sky'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative, depending on tone; it can sound affectionate when used about friends
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'nutty' informally to describe a person who acts wildly or a plan that seems silly. It is friendly in casual talk, but it can be rude if used about someone's mental health. For food, 'nutty' describes flavors like roasted almonds or peanut butter, and it is pleasant and neutral.

distinctions.note: 'Crazy' is stronger and more common, while 'nutty' is milder, playful, and more informal.

examples.everyday: My roommate had a nutty idea to paint the whole kitchen purple at midnight.
examples.professional: The nutty proposal to rewrite the entire database over a weekend was rejected by the team.
examples.analytical: The philosopher dismissed the nutty theory as internally inconsistent, not merely eccentric.

nuance.analogy: Like a hazelnut shell: the word's playful sound suggests something quirky and a little cracked.
nuance.etymology: From 'nut' (Old English hnutu) with the suffix '-y'; the sense of 'crazy' developed from the older slang 'nuts'.
common_mistakes: Using 'nutty' for serious mental illness, which can sound offensive.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'nut-TEE'.

conversation.text: Brown rice has a nice nutty flavor.
Toasting the bread gives it a nutty taste.
My uncle has some nutty ideas about cooking.

senses.definition: A type of lever used to propel a boat, having a flat blade at one end and a handle at the other, and pivoted in a rowlock atop the gunwale, whereby a rower seated in the boat and pulling the handle can pass the blade through the water by repeated strokes against the water's resistance, thus moving the boat.
An oarsman; a rower.
senses.example: He is a good oar.

senses.definition: An oar-like swimming organ of various invertebrates.
To row; to travel with, or as if with, oars.

core.definition: A long pole with a flat blade at one end, used to row and move a boat by pushing against the water.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is the open 'aw' sound of 'caught' in General American, and the r is strongly pronounced. Do not add a second syllable or pronounce the silent 'a' as a separate sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'oar' for the paddle-like tool that is held in rowlocks, mainly for rowing boats. For a canoe or kayak, Americans usually say 'paddle' instead, which is a single-bladed or double-bladed tool held in the hands without a pivot. 'Oar' is also common in phrases like 'rest on your oars' meaning to stop working.

distinctions.note: An oar is pivoted on a fixed point (oarlock or rowlock) on the boat, while a paddle is held freely in the hands and used in canoes and kayaks.
A rudder steers a boat from the stern, whereas an oar propels it forward.

examples.everyday: We rented a little rowboat at the lake, and my son insisted on holding the oars the whole way.
examples.professional: The rental company requires that every customer receive a lesson on how to handle the oars before leaving the dock.
examples.analytical: Homer's ships are propelled by oars and sails, and the rhythm of rowing structures the narrative's images of labor and return.

nuance.analogy: An oar is like a lever in water: the handle pushes the blade back, and the blade pushes the water back, so the boat moves forward.
nuance.etymology: From Old English 'ar', related to Old Norse 'ár'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like 'oh-ar' with two syllables; it is one syllable.
Using 'oar' for a canoe paddle, which Americans call a paddle.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture, oars appear in descriptions of ships. The Hebrew word 'mashot' is used in Ezekiel 27:6, where the oars of the ships of Tire are made of oaks of Bashan. Ezekiel 27:29 describes the men who handle the oars leaving the ships in lament. Isaiah 33:21 pictures the LORD as a place of broad rivers where no galley with oars can pass, a figure of safety from enemies.

oar.etymology: From Middle English *ore* (“oar”), from Old English *ār*, from **airu*, from Proto-Germanic **airō* (“oar”).

senses.definition: A metaphysical doctrine that holds that all events are occasioned (caused) by God.
A nonce word.

core.definition: The philosophical view that God is the only true cause, and that events we think cause each other are only occasions for divine action.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the 'kay' syllable. The '-sion' in 'occasion' is pronounced 'zhun,' and the final syllables are reduced, so they sound like 'um.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical term in philosophy and history of ideas.
nuance.usage_note: Americans encounter occasionalism in college philosophy courses, especially when studying Descartes, Malebranche, and the problem of causation. It is not used in everyday talk, but a philosophy student might discuss it in seminar or in a paper.

distinctions.note: Occasional is an everyday adjective meaning happening now and then. Occasionalism is a technical philosophical doctrine about causation.
Determinism holds that events follow necessarily from prior causes. Occasionalism holds that God, not natural causes, produces the effects we observe.

examples.professional: The reading group argued that occasionalism, though elegant, offers little practical guidance for modeling real causal systems.
examples.analytical: Malebranche's occasionalism answers Hume's problem of causation by locating all true causal power in God's will.

nuance.analogy: Like a puppeteer whose hand moves each puppet, occasionalism says the real action comes from God, and the apparent causes merely signal when God acts.
nuance.etymology: From Latin occasio, 'opportunity, occasion,' with the suffix -ism, a doctrine or system.
common_mistakes: Confusing occasionalism with the everyday adjective occasional.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'oc-CA-sion-al-ism.'

core.definition: The first part of the Christian Bible, containing the Hebrew Scriptures written before Jesus, which Christians share with Judaism.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress is on 'TES'. The last two syllables are reduced to 'tuh-munt'. The d in 'old' links softly to 'test'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; some Jewish readers and scholars prefer 'Hebrew Bible' because 'Old' may imply replacement.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term in churches, schools, and everyday talk. 'Old Testament' is also used figuratively for harsh or stern things, as in 'Old Testament justice'. In interfaith or academic settings, 'Hebrew Bible' is often preferred.

distinctions.note: Hebrew Bible is the Jewish name and a neutral scholarly term; Old Testament is the Christian name and its order and contents can differ.
Tanakh is the Jewish acronym for Torah, Prophets, and Writings, arranged differently from the Christian Old Testament.
The New Testament contains the Gospels, Acts, letters, and Revelation.

collocations: the Old Testament and the New

examples.everyday: We're reading through the Old Testament this year in our church group.
examples.professional: This course surveys Old Testament theology from Genesis to the prophets.
examples.analytical: Christians read the Old Testament as the story of promise that finds fulfillment in Christ, a reading Jewish interpreters do not share.

nuance.analogy: The Old Testament is the first act of a two-part story: Christians see the second act as its fulfillment.
nuance.etymology: From Latin vetus testamentum, 'old covenant'; Greek diatheke can mean covenant or will.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'testament' with a full 'ment' vowel instead of 'munt'.
Thinking 'Old' means outdated or unimportant.
Omitting the article: 'in Old Testament' instead of 'in the Old Testament'.
nuance.biblical_note: The phrase 'old covenant' appears in 2 Corinthians 3:14, where Paul speaks of reading the old covenant. Jeremiah 31:31 promises a new covenant, which Hebrews 8:8-13 applies to Christ. In Matthew 5:17, Jesus says he came to fulfill the Law and the Prophets, not abolish them.

traditions.view: The Old Testament usually follows the Septuagint and includes additional books such as Wisdom and Tobit. It is read in worship as pointing to Christ.
The Old Testament has 46 books, including the deuterocanonical books, and is read as one with the New in God's plan.
The Old Testament has 39 books, matching the Hebrew canon. Protestants differ on how the Law applies to Christians, with Lutheran, Reformed, and dispensational views varying.

old-testament.etymology: From Middle English *Olde Testament*, calqued from Latin *Vetus Testāmentum*.

senses.definition: Running AI models directly on a phone, laptop or other device rather than in the cloud.

core.definition: Running AI models directly on a phone, laptop, or other device instead of sending data to remote cloud servers.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on VICE in 'device' and on EYE in 'AI', which is spoken as the letters A and I. The vowel in 'device' is reduced in the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive in tech contexts. It suggests privacy, speed, and offline capability.
nuance.usage_note: Engineers and product managers in the US use this phrase when discussing privacy, latency, or battery use. A natural reply is 'Does the app need internet, or is it on-device?' It is a technical term but increasingly known to general audiences through phone marketing. Americans say the letters A-I, not the word 'ay'.

distinctions.note: Cloud AI sends data to remote servers for processing; on-device AI processes data locally, which can improve privacy and speed but is limited by device hardware.
Edge AI is a broader term for processing at the network edge, including gateways and sensors; on-device AI refers specifically to the device itself.

examples.everyday: My new phone does voice translation on-device, so it still works when I'm on a plane.
examples.professional: We're moving the image classifier to on-device AI to cut latency and reduce server costs.
examples.analytical: On-device AI shifts some privacy questions from corporate data centers to the individual's hardware, though it does not eliminate them.

nuance.analogy: Like cooking dinner in your own kitchen instead of ordering delivery from a restaurant across town.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'AI' as one syllable like 'eye' with a long vowel only; it is spoken as two letters, A and I.
Writing 'on device AI' without hyphens in technical writing; the compound adjective is normally 'on-device'.

conversation.text: On-device AI runs models directly on phones or laptops instead of in the cloud.
On-device AI keeps personal data local and works without an internet connection.
On-device AI forces us to use small, quantized models because of memory and battery limits.

senses.definition: Of or relating to ontology.
Of or pertaining to the nature of being or existence.

core.definition: Relating to ontology, the philosophical study of what exists and the basic nature of being.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on LAH, the third syllable, and the -gi- sound is a soft j. Say ahn-tuh-LAH-jih-kul, with a flap or soft t in the middle.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It signals careful, abstract thought in philosophy or theology.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ontological in philosophy, theology, and computer science. In casual talk, people would say about the nature of reality or what things really are. It can sound pretentious in everyday conversation, so save it for academic or technical settings.

distinctions.note: Ontological concerns the theory or structure of being, while ontic concerns particular beings and their actual existence.
Ontological concerns what exists, while epistemological concerns how we know what exists.

examples.everyday: I'm not sure what you mean by a number being real, so give me an ontological question I can understand.
examples.professional: Before we design the schema, we need an ontological agreement on what counts as a customer.
examples.analytical: The paper argues that the theory has an ontological commitment to abstract objects, which the author never fully justifies.

nuance.analogy: Ontological thinking is like asking what kinds of things a city contains before you start mapping its streets.
nuance.etymology: From Greek on, ontos, being, and logia, study of.
common_mistakes: Confusing ontological with epistemological, which concerns knowledge rather than existence.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in ahn-tuh-LOJ-ih-kul, which sounds unnatural.

senses.definition: Overly bossy, domineering, arrogant, forceful, intense, or annoying.

core.definition: Overly bossy and domineering; forcing your opinions or authority on others in an arrogant way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on BEAR, the third syllable, and the "-ing" is a short, unstressed ending. Avoid stressing the first syllable, which is a common error with compound words.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a person who dominates others and is hard to work with.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this to describe bosses, parents, or neighbors who take over conversations or decisions. It can be used in calm criticism, such as "My manager is a bit overbearing." Avoid it in very polite company when speaking directly to someone, since it sounds like a judgment of their character.

distinctions.note: Bossy is informal and mostly about giving orders; overbearing is stronger and suggests intimidating others with pressure or arrogance.
Domineering is close in meaning and focuses on controlling others; overbearing adds the sense of being tiresomely forceful in manner.

examples.everyday: My sister is kind, but she can get overbearing when she plans our family trips.
examples.professional: Several engineers said the lead was overbearing in code reviews, so the team now rotates who leads them.
examples.analytical: Philosophers have long warned that a state can become overbearing when it claims authority over conscience.

nuance.analogy: Like a loud speaker who fills the room so completely that no one else can be heard.
nuance.etymology: From "overbear," from "over" plus "bear," meaning to press down or overpower.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with "overbearing" meaning heavy in weight; in everyday use it is about personality.
Stressing the first syllable, as in "OH-vur-bair-ing"; the main stress is on BAIR.

senses.definition: To subdue someone by superior force.
senses.example: We overpowered the opposing army within a couple of hours.

senses.definition: To excel or exceed in power; to cause to yield; to subdue.
senses.example: Bright light overpowers the eyes.

senses.definition: To render imperceptible by means of greater strength, intensity, etc.
senses.example: The dish was OK, but the garlic slightly overpowered the herbs.

senses.definition: To make excessively powerful.

core.definition: To defeat or overcome someone or something by using greater strength, force, or influence.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, -POW-, which rhymes with 'now'. The final syllable is a reduced American 'er', so say 'POW-er' without a strong final vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral; it can describe violence, unfair force, or overwhelming effects.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'overpower' for physical struggles, like police subduing a suspect, and for overwhelming feelings, like 'The smell overpowered me.' In casual speech, 'overwhelm' or 'take over' is also common. Avoid using it for a mild victory in a game, where 'beat' is more natural.

distinctions.note: 'Overwhelm' focuses on feelings or large numbers; 'overpower' focuses on force or strength applied directly.
'Defeat' is a general word for winning; 'overpower' suggests greater force or strength was used.

examples.everyday: The smell of the bakery was so strong that it almost overpowered me at the door.
examples.professional: The vendor's sales pitch overpowered our team, so we didn't ask the hard questions about cost.
examples.analytical: Religious authority can overpower individual conscience, which is why many traditions insist on personal discernment.

nuance.analogy: Like a loud speaker drowning out a quiet voice, something that overpowers simply has more force, so the other thing cannot be heard or felt.
nuance.etymology: From over + power.
common_mistakes: Using 'overpower' to mean 'overcome a problem' with logic; it usually means force or strength.
Stressing the first syllable, as in 'OH-ver-pow-er'.

senses.definition: Excessively nervous, excited, tense, angry, anxious, or upset; overemotional; very uneasy.
Elaborate; baroque; overdone.

core.definition: Extremely nervous, anxious, or upset, so that your emotions are out of control.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the final syllable, 'RAWT', with the r pronounced clearly in American speech. The vowel is the 'aw' sound from cot-caught merger speakers, so 'rawt' rhymes with 'thought'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes excessive emotion, often in a way that seems unreasonable.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use overwrought mainly in writing, reviews, and descriptive speech, not in casual conversation. It often describes a person who is too emotional about a situation. In everyday talk, people more often say 'really upset' or 'freaking out'.

distinctions.note: Upset is common and general, while overwrought suggests a more intense emotional state that seems excessive.
Anxious describes worry about the future, while overwrought describes a more intense, sometimes out-of-control, emotional response.

examples.everyday: Don't get so overwrought about the wedding; the flowers will be fine.
examples.professional: The client was overwrought after the outage, so we need a calm and clear status update.
examples.analytical: The essay's overwrought prose buries its argument under so many images that the reader loses the thread.

nuance.analogy: An overwrought person is like a kettle boiling over, with emotion spilling out faster than it can be contained.
nuance.etymology: From 'over' and the archaic past participle 'wrought' of the verb 'work', meaning worked or shaped too much.
common_mistakes: Using overwrought as a synonym for overworked, which is a different meaning.
Confusing it with wrought iron, which is a noun phrase about metal and not related to emotion.

senses.definition: A state in which one is logically compelled to contradict oneself.
An apparently self-contradictory statement, which can only be true if it is false, and vice versa.
senses.example: "This sentence is false" is a paradox.

senses.definition: A counterintuitive conclusion or outcome.
senses.example: It is an interesting paradox that drinking a lot of water can often make you feel thirsty.

senses.definition: A claim that two apparently contradictory ideas are true.
senses.example: Not having a fashion is a fashion; that's a paradox.

senses.definition: A thing involving contradictory yet interrelated elements that exist simultaneously and persist over time.
A person or thing having contradictory properties.
senses.example: He is a paradox; you would not expect him in that political party.

senses.definition: An unanswerable question or difficult puzzle, particularly one which leads to a deeper truth.
The use of counterintuitive or contradictory statements (paradoxes) in speech or writing.
The practice of giving instructions that are opposed to the therapist's actual intent, with the intention that the client will disobey or be unable to obey.

core.definition: A statement or situation that seems self-contradictory or absurd but may still contain a truth or an explanation.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, PAR. The final vowel is the 'o' of 'hot' or 'cot', not the 'o' of 'ox'. The American pronunciation uses the rhotic r clearly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a puzzle or a surprising truth, and it can be intellectual or playful.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'paradox' in essays, science writing and ordinary conversation to point out something that seems contradictory, like 'It's a paradox: the more we work, the less time we have.' It is not a casual word for surprise; for a plain contradiction, Americans often say 'contradiction' or 'irony'. It sounds natural in discussions about logic, life or society.

distinctions.note: A contradiction is a flat logical inconsistency that cannot be true; a paradox seems contradictory but may still be true on closer analysis.
Irony is saying the opposite of what you mean for effect; a paradox is a statement or situation that looks self-contradictory in itself.

examples.everyday: It's a paradox, but I feel more rested when I get up earlier.
examples.professional: There's a paradox here: our dashboards show more data than ever, yet nobody trusts the numbers.
examples.analytical: Zeno's paradox of motion argues that a runner can never reach the finish line, yet the argument seems to contradict observation, which is why it has inspired so much philosophy.

nuance.analogy: A paradox is like a magic trick: it looks impossible at first, but a careful look shows how it works.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin paradoxum, from Greek paradoxos, 'contrary to opinion or expectation', from para, 'beyond', and doxa, 'opinion'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in 'pa-RAD-ox'.
Using paradox for any simple surprise; in everyday talk, 'irony' or 'funny thing is' is often more natural.

paradox.etymology: From Middle French *paradoxe*, from Latin *paradoxum*, from Ancient Greek *παράδοξος* (“unexpected, strange”).

senses.definition: Someone suffering from paralysis.
A drug that produces paralysis.
Affected by paralysis; paralyzed.
Pertaining to paralysis.

core.definition: A person who is unable to move part or all of the body because of paralysis.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on LIT, the third syllable, and the final -ic is pronounced 'ik'. Learners often give the first syllable too much stress or pronounce the ending as 'ick'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: In modern American English, paralytic is mostly used as an adjective, and as a noun it sounds old-fashioned. Americans today more often say 'a person with paralysis' or 'a paralyzed person', which sounds kinder. The word appears often in Bible study and Scripture discussions, where it is the standard translation.

distinctions.note: Paralytic is more formal or clinical in tone, while paralyzed is the common everyday word.
Lame refers to difficulty walking, while paralytic means loss of movement, and the term lame can sound dated or insulting today.

examples.everyday: My neighbor, who had a stroke, sits at the window every morning, so we bring her coffee.
examples.professional: The nursing protocol requires that paralytic patients be repositioned every two hours to prevent pressure sores.
examples.analytical: In Mark's Gospel, the paralytic becomes a symbol of human helplessness that Jesus addresses before he addresses the physical need.

nuance.analogy: Like a car with its engine running but its wheels locked, unable to move forward.
nuance.etymology: From Greek paralytikos, from paraluein, to loosen at the side.
common_mistakes: Using paralytic as an everyday adjective for being very tired or drunk, which sounds wrong.
Stressing the first syllable instead of LIT.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word is paralytikos (παραλυτικός), from paraluein, to loosen at the side, meaning a person weakened or disabled in limb. Three Gospel accounts describe Jesus healing a paralytic: Mark 2:1-12 tells of four men lowering a paralytic through a roof, and Jesus first forgives his sins before healing him. Matthew 9:1-8 gives a parallel account in which Jesus says to the man to rise and walk, and the crowd glorifies God. Luke 5:17-26 offers a third account in which the healing reveals Jesus' authority to forgive sins.

paralytic.etymology: French *paralytique*, from Latin *paralyticus*, from Ancient Greek *παραλυτικός* (“paralyzed”).

senses.definition: The second coming of Christ.

core.definition: The Greek theological term for the second coming of Christ in glory at the end of the age, meaning his 'presence' or 'arrival.'

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, ROO. The s between vowels is voiced like z, and the final -ia is a quick 'zee-uh,' not 'see-ah.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to reverent; it is a technical theological term, hopeful in Christian contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word almost only in theology, seminary classes, and scholarly writing. Most people say 'the Second Coming' instead. Using it in casual talk would sound very academic, though pastors may use it in teaching.

distinctions.note: 'Second coming' is the common English phrase; 'parousia' is the Greek technical term, often used to stress the idea of arrival and presence.
'Advent' means any arrival, and in Christianity refers to Christ's first coming and the season before Christmas, while 'parousia' is the final return.
'Epiphany' means a manifestation or revelation, often of Christ at his first coming, whereas 'parousia' is his future return.

examples.everyday: My seminary friend keeps saying 'parousia,' and I finally asked him if that just means the Second Coming.
examples.professional: In today's lecture, we will look at how Paul describes the parousia in 1 Thessalonians.
examples.analytical: Early Christian communities lived in tension between the hope of an imminent parousia and the need to build lasting institutions.

nuance.analogy: Like the arrival of a king in a city, with the whole city gathered to greet him.
nuance.etymology: From Greek parousia, 'presence, arrival,' from para- 'beside' + ousia 'being.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'PAR-oo-see-uh' with stress on the first syllable.
Pronouncing the s as /s/ instead of /z/.
Using it for any arrival, rather than only the return of Christ.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek parousia means 'presence' or 'coming.' It is used for Christ's return in Matthew 24:3, where the disciples ask about the sign of his coming; in 1 Thessalonians 4:15, where Paul says believers who are alive at the coming will not precede those who have died; and in 1 Corinthians 15:23, where those who belong to Christ are raised at his coming.

senses.definition: Fearful, timid.

core.definition: Literary word meaning fearful or timid, lacking courage.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a short, reduced 'ih' sound, not 'eed'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a state of fear or timidity, usually with a tone of disapproval or poetic description.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this word outside poetry, older religious writing or deliberate literary style. In conversation you would say 'timid', 'scared' or 'fearful'. Using it in speech may sound affected or old-fashioned.

distinctions.note: Timid is common everyday English for shy or easily frightened; pavid is archaic and literary.
Fearful is the normal modern word for full of fear; pavid is more poetic and less used.

examples.everyday: My grandfather, who read old poetry aloud, called a nervous little dog pavid, and we all laughed.
examples.professional: The editor cut the word pavid from the memo because the team preferred plain words like 'timid'.
examples.analytical: The poet's pavid speaker reveals a spiritual anxiety that the later stanzas attempt to resolve.

nuance.analogy: A pavid person is like a bird that freezes at every sound in the bushes.
nuance.etymology: From Latin pavidus, afraid, from pavere, to fear.
common_mistakes: Using pavid in everyday speech where timid or scared sounds natural.
Stressing the second syllable instead of the first.

senses.definition: (rare) To embezzle.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: To steal money or property entrusted to your care, especially public funds or an employer's funds.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, PEK. The middle syllables are reduced to a quick schwa, so say PEK-yuh-layt, not pek-yoo-LAYT.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a serious crime against public trust.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in legal, journalistic, and academic writing about government or institutional theft. In casual speech people say steal, embezzle, or misuse funds. Using peculate in conversation may sound stiff, but it is correct in reports and formal articles.

distinctions.note: Embezzle is the common American legal and business word for stealing money from an employer or organization; peculate is rarer and historically tied to public funds.
Steal is general and informal; peculate specifies the theft of funds held in trust or in a public office.

examples.everyday: The news said the mayor's aide had peculated city money, and everyone at the diner was talking about it.
examples.professional: The auditor found that the treasurer had peculated several thousand dollars from the nonprofit's reserve account.
examples.analytical: Historians argue that the reform laws were written to stop officials from peculating funds that were meant for the public good.

nuance.analogy: To peculate is to quietly take water from a shared well that you were hired to guard.
nuance.etymology: From Latin peculatus, past participle of peculari, to embezzle, from peculium, private property, from pecus, cattle.
common_mistakes: Using peculate for theft by a stranger; it applies only to someone trusted with the funds.
Confusing it with peculiar, which is unrelated in meaning.

peculate.etymology: From Latin *pecūlātus*, past participle of *pecūlor* (“defraud, embezzle”).

senses.definition: Any of various seabirds of the family Pelecanidae, having a long bill with a distendable pouch.
A native or resident of the American state of Louisiana.
A retort or still having a curved tube or tubes leading back from the head to the body for continuous condensation and redistillation.
A waterbomber.
An ageing prostitute.
A set of forceps used to force overcrowded teeth apart.

core.definition: A large water bird with a long bill and a throat pouch that it uses to scoop up fish.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, PEL. The middle syllables are quick and reduced, so the word ends in a soft kun.

nuance.connotation: Neutral or positive. It is a familiar bird, and in Christian symbolism it can suggest self-sacrificing love.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pelican as an everyday word for the bird, especially in Florida, Louisiana and along the coast. In Louisiana, Pelican is also the state nickname, and a resident may be called a Pelican. In Bible study, be aware that the Hebrew word may refer to a different bird than the English one.

distinctions.note: A cormorant is a dark, long-necked diving bird without a pouch that holds fish, while a pelican has the large bill pouch.
A seagull is a smaller, common coastal bird, while a pelican is much larger and has a distinctive bill pouch.

examples.everyday: We saw a few pelicans diving off the pier in Florida, and my kids couldn't stop watching them.
examples.professional: The coastal survey notes that pelican nesting sites were relocated after the storm.
examples.analytical: In Psalm 102 the psalmist likens his loneliness to that of a pelican in the wilderness, a bird of solitary places.

nuance.analogy: A pelican is like a fishing net with a built-in pocket: it scoops up fish and holds them until it is ready to swallow.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin pelicanus, from Greek pelekan, probably related to pelekys, 'axe', perhaps for the shape of the bill.
common_mistakes: Confusing the bird with the Louisiana resident sense when speaking casually; context usually makes it clear.
Stressing the last syllable, as in 'pel-ih-KAN'.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word qa'ath, translated pelican in the Revised Standard Version, appears in Leviticus 11:18 and Deuteronomy 14:17 in lists of unclean birds. Psalm 102:6 compares the psalmist's lonely condition to a pelican of the wilderness. Scholars are not certain the Hebrew word refers to the bird we call a pelican, and some suggest a different wilderness bird.

pelican.etymology: From Middle English *pellican*, *pellicane*, from Old English *pellican* (“pelican”), from Latin *pelecānus*, from Ancient Greek *πελεκάν*

senses.definition: Awaiting a conclusion or a confirmation.
Begun but not completed.
About to happen; imminent or impending.
While waiting for something; until.
senses.example: Pending the outcome of the investigation, the police officer is suspended from duty.

senses.definition: During.
senses.example: Pending the investigation, the police officer is suspended from duty.

core.definition: Not yet decided, approved, or completed; waiting for a result, decision, or confirmation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, PEN-. The -ing ending is a short, light 'ing', not a long 'eeng'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a status without judging it, though it can imply delay or uncertainty.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pending constantly in business, legal, and government contexts, as in 'The application is pending.' In casual speech they often say 'still waiting' or 'not decided yet' instead. As a preposition, pending is formal, as in 'pending approval'.

distinctions.note: Undecided describes a person's mind, while pending describes a process or request that is waiting for an outcome.
Until is neutral and common, while pending is formal and often used in writing about official processes.

examples.everyday: My loan is still pending, so I cannot buy the car yet.
examples.professional: The ticket is still pending review, so we will update the client once the team signs off.
examples.analytical: The verdict remains pending, which means the court has not yet decided whether the statute applies.

nuance.analogy: Pending is like a package that has shipped but has not arrived yet: the outcome exists, but it is still on its way.
nuance.etymology: From Latin pendere 'to hang, weigh', via the sense of a matter hanging undecided.
common_mistakes: Using pending for a person who is undecided, as in 'I am pending about the job'.
Using pending as a verb instead of an adjective or preposition.

senses.definition: Any function whose value repeats after the regular addition of a period to its independent variable; i.e. a function ƒ such that, for some positive constant p, ƒ(x + p) = ƒ(x) for all x.

core.definition: A function whose values repeat after a fixed period p, so that f(x + p) equals f(x) for every x.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the AH in periodic and the FUNGK in function. The word periodic has the same stress pattern as in everyday English, and -tion is pronounced shun.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise mathematical term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use periodic function in math, physics, engineering, and signal processing classes and work. The sine and cosine functions are the standard examples. In casual talk you would rarely use the term, but a student or engineer would say it naturally when discussing waves or repeating signals.

distinctions.note: A periodic function is the mathematical object, while a periodic signal is the same idea applied to a physical or time-varying quantity in engineering.
An oscillation is a back-and-forth motion in physics, while a periodic function is an abstract mathematical description that may or may not describe a physical oscillation.

collocations: a periodic function with period p
the fundamental period of a periodic function

examples.everyday: My brother is studying engineering, and he said a sine wave is a periodic function that keeps repeating the same shape.
examples.professional: Before we apply the Fourier transform to the sensor data, we need to confirm that the signal is a periodic function with a known period.
examples.analytical: A function f is periodic with period p if f(x + p) = f(x) for all x, and the least such positive p is called the fundamental period.

nuance.analogy: A periodic function is like a song on repeat: after one full period, the same melody returns exactly as before.
nuance.etymology: Periodic from Greek periodikos, 'recurring'; function from Latin functio, 'performance, execution.'
common_mistakes: Saying periodic function when the function is only approximately repeating, which is not the same as exactly periodic.
Stressing the wrong syllable in periodic, as in PEER-ee-AH-dik.

senses.definition: To make (something) perpetual; to make (something) continue for an indefinite time; also, to preserve (something) from extinction or oblivion.
To prolong the existence of (something) by repetition; to reinforce.
To record (the testimony of a witness) which may be lost before a matter comes to trial.

core.definition: To cause something to continue or recur for a long time, often when it should end, such as a stereotype, a problem or a tradition.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, PET, and the final -ate is a full vowel rather than a reduced one. Many learners say the middle as puh-PET or stress the last syllable, so practice per-PET-chuh-wayt.

nuance.connotation: Usually negative when the thing perpetuated is a problem, such as bias or myths. It can be neutral or positive for traditions and good practices.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use perpetuate in school, workplace and news contexts to say that something harmful or unfair keeps going, as in perpetuating stereotypes. In casual speech people more often say keep something going or keep it up. The word sounds formal in a casual conversation, so use it in writing, meetings and debates.

distinctions.note: Continue is neutral and everyday; perpetuate adds the idea that something is being deliberately or systematically kept alive, often with consequences.
Maintain means to keep something in good condition or at a standard; perpetuate implies prolonging something that may be undesirable or outdated.

examples.everyday: My uncle keeps telling those old jokes, and I think he is perpetuating stereotypes without realizing it.
examples.professional: If we train the model on last year's hiring data, we risk perpetuating the same bias in our recommendations.
examples.analytical: Institutions often perpetuate inequality not through open hostility but through procedures that seem neutral.

nuance.analogy: Like a rumor passed from person to person, a perpetuated idea keeps moving because each person repeats it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin perpetuare, from perpetuus, meaning continuous or uninterrupted.
common_mistakes: Saying perpetuate something when you mean repeat it once; perpetuate implies continuing over time.
Mispronouncing the stress as per-puh-TYOO-ate or stressing the last syllable.

perpetuate.etymology: (16th century) From earlier perpetuat, Latin *perpetuātus* (“perpetuated”), perfect passive participle of *perpetuō* (“to cause to continue uninterruptedly, to proceed with continually, to make perpetual, perpetuate”) (see *-ate*), from *perpetuus* + *-ō*,…

senses.definition: Having undergone the process of petrification (transformation into a stony substance); turned to stone.
Extremely afraid.

core.definition: Extremely frightened, so scared that you cannot move or think clearly; also used literally for wood or bone turned into stone.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and reduce the middle vowel to a quick 'uh'. Keep the 'r' strong, and make the final syllable a clear 'fyde'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes intense fear, though in the literal sense of fossilized material it is neutral.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech, 'petrified' usually means terrified, as in 'I was petrified of the dentist'. It is casual and expressive. The literal sense of 'turned to stone' is mainly used by geologists, paleontologists and science writers. Use 'terrified' in formal writing to avoid sounding overly dramatic.

distinctions.note: Petrified suggests being frozen by fear and is more colloquial; terrified is neutral and suitable for formal writing.
Scared is mild and everyday, while petrified implies a much stronger fear that paralyzes you.

examples.everyday: I was petrified when the dog ran toward me in the park.
examples.professional: Our junior engineers were petrified of presenting the outage report to the executives.
examples.analytical: The fossil was a petrified specimen, its organic tissue replaced by mineral over millions of years.

nuance.analogy: Like a statue that cannot move, a petrified person freezes completely under fear.
nuance.etymology: From the verb petrify, from Greek petra 'stone' and Latin facere 'to make'.
common_mistakes: Using petrified for mild worry, as in 'I was petrified about the test', which sounds too strong.
Pronouncing the middle syllable as 'tri' instead of a reduced 'ruh'.

senses.definition: Something that portends an event about to occur, especially an unfortunate or evil event; an omen.
senses.example: It was a portent of things to come.

senses.definition: A portending; significance.
senses.example: a howl of dire portent

senses.definition: Something regarded as portentous; a marvel; prodigy.

core.definition: A sign or warning that something important, especially something bad, is going to happen.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The second syllable is a weak schwa, so it sounds like "tuhnt" and not "tent."

nuance.connotation: Often negative, suggesting an ominous sign; occasionally neutral when describing a remarkable omen.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use portent in writing or formal speech, often in phrases like a portent of doom or an ominous portent. It is less common in casual talk, where people usually say sign, warning or bad omen. The word can sound dramatic if used for minor matters.

distinctions.note: Omen is a broader and more common word for any sign of the future; portent is more formal and often suggests a serious or ominous sign.
Sign is neutral and everyday; portent implies a warning of something significant.

examples.everyday: That loud crack in the ceiling was a portent of trouble, so we called the landlord.
examples.professional: Flat sales in the first quarter were a portent of the budget cuts coming in the fall.
examples.analytical: In classical thought, a portent was read as evidence of a larger moral order, and its meaning depended on the community that interpreted it.

nuance.analogy: A portent is like thunder before a storm: the sound arrives first, and it tells you what is probably coming.
nuance.etymology: From Latin portentum, sign or omen, from portendere, to portend.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the second syllable as "tent" with a clear e.
Using portent as a verb; the verb is portend.

portent.etymology: Borrowed from Latin *portentum*, participle of *portendere*, from *portendō* (“to predict, to foretell”).

senses.definition: Fired ceramic wares that contain clay when formed.
senses.example: The shelves were lined with pottery of all shapes and sizes.

senses.definition: A potter's shop or workshop, where pottery is made.
senses.example: I visited the old potteries and saw the pots being made.

senses.definition: The potter's craft or art: making vessels from clay.
senses.example: Bernard Leach was skilled at pottery.

core.definition: Objects such as bowls, jars, and plates made from clay and hardened by firing; also the craft of making them.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, PAH. The middle syllable is a weak schwa, and the t between vowels is flapped so it sounds close to a soft d. The final syllable is a light ee sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive; the word suggests craftsmanship, handmade art, and everyday household objects.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pottery both for the finished ceramic objects and for the craft itself, as in taking a pottery class. It is uncountable in the sense of objects, but you can say a piece of pottery. Americans often say pottery studio or pottery shop for the workplace, and ceramics for the broader category in art and industry.

distinctions.note: Ceramics is the broader category covering all fired clay and related materials, including tiles, bricks, and industrial parts; pottery refers to vessels and household wares.
Porcelain is a fine, white, translucent ceramic made at very high heat; pottery can be coarse earthenware or stoneware.

examples.everyday: My sister took a pottery class on Saturdays and now she makes mugs for the whole family.
examples.professional: Our product design team reviewed the pottery line's glaze samples before the spring catalog.
examples.analytical: The distribution of decorated pottery across the valley suggests a shared trade network among its communities.

nuance.analogy: Pottery is like a handwritten letter in clay: the shape, the glaze, and the marks all carry the maker's hand.
nuance.etymology: From pottery, from the word potter, from Old English pottere, a maker of pots; the suffix -ery denotes a place or work.
common_mistakes: Using 'pottery' as a countable noun for one item; say 'a piece of pottery' or 'a pot' instead.
Confusing 'pottery' with 'potter's shop'; in American English, a pottery can be a workshop, but in casual talk it usually means the objects.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word yotser (יוֹצֵר) means potter or one who forms, and the Greek word kerameus (κεραμεύς) means potter. Jeremiah 18:6 uses the potter and his clay to illustrate God's authority over Israel. Romans 9:21 asks whether the potter does not have authority over the clay, to make from the same lump one vessel for honor and another for dishonor.

pottery.etymology: From Old French *poterie*, from *potier* (“potter”), from the root of *pot*, equivalent to *pot* + *ery*.

senses.definition: That which precurses: a forerunner, predecessor, or indicator of approaching events.
One of the compounds that participates in the chemical reaction that produces another compound.
Caused by the following symbol.

core.definition: Something that comes before and leads to or indicates something later; a forerunner.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, -KUR-, and the final syllable is a weak 'ur'. Do not pronounce it 'pre-KUR-soar' with a separate 'or' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a relationship in time or cause without praise or blame.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'precursor' in news, business, science and history to describe early versions or signs of something. It is more formal than 'forerunner' and commonly appears in phrases like 'a precursor to the crisis'. In casual talk, people often say 'the first version' or 'the start of'.

distinctions.note: A 'predecessor' is a person who held a role before someone else; a 'precursor' is a thing, idea or sign that came before and led to something.
'Forerunner' is a near-synonym with a more literary tone; 'precursor' is more common in technical and academic writing.

examples.everyday: That little argument at dinner was a precursor to the bigger fight we had on Sunday.
examples.professional: The small outage last week was a precursor to the bigger failure, so we need to review the alert logs.
examples.analytical: Early Enlightenment debates about natural rights were a precursor to the modern concept of human dignity.

nuance.analogy: Dark clouds before a storm: they are not the storm itself, but they reliably signal that it is coming.
nuance.etymology: From Latin praecursor, 'a forerunner', from praecurrere 'to run before', from prae 'before' and currere 'to run'.
common_mistakes: Using 'precursor' as an adjective; the adjective form is 'precursory', which is rare. Use 'precursor' as a noun and 'preceding' or 'earlier' in most adjective uses.
Confusing 'precursor' with 'predecessor' when speaking about a person who held a job earlier.

precursor.etymology: Middle English *precursour*, from Middle French *precurseur* or its etymon Latin *praecursor*.

senses.definition: A false, contrived, or assumed purpose or reason; a pretense.
senses.example: The reporter called the company on the pretext of trying to resolve a consumer complaint.

senses.definition: To employ a pretext, which involves using a false or contrived purpose for soliciting the gain of something else.
senses.example: The spy obtained his phone records using possibly-illegal pretexting methods.

core.definition: A false or made-up reason given to hide the real reason for doing something.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, PREE. The final 'xt' is a clear 'kst' sound, so the word has two syllables, not three.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies deception or a cover story.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'pretext' in news, business, and everyday conversation to say someone used a false excuse, such as 'They used a broken light as a pretext to stop me.' It is slightly formal. In casual speech people often say 'an excuse' or 'a cover story'. The phrase 'on the pretext of' is common and natural.

distinctions.note: An excuse can be honest or false, and is everyday; a pretext is always a false reason hiding the real motive.
Pretense is the act of pretending or the general appearance of something; pretext is a specific false reason used to justify an action.

examples.everyday: He called me just on the pretext of asking about the game, but he really wanted to talk about the job.
examples.professional: The manager used the reorganization as a pretext to cut the team, although the budget had not changed.
examples.analytical: Scholars argue that the stated doctrinal concern was merely a pretext for the political purge that followed.

nuance.analogy: Like a movie set front: it looks like a real building from the street, but behind it is something different.
nuance.etymology: From Latin praetextus, 'pretext, pretense', from praetexere, 'to weave in front, to cover'.
common_mistakes: Using 'pretext' for an honest reason; it always implies a false cover.
Saying 'pretext to' instead of 'pretext for' when giving the purpose.

pretext.etymology: From Latin *praetextum* (“an ornament, etc. wrought in front, a pretense”), neuter of *praetextus*, past participle of *praetexō* (“to weave before, fringe or border, allege”).

senses.definition: The legal process of verifying the legality of a will.
A copy of a legally recognized and qualified will.
Clipping of probate court.
To establish the legality of (a will).

core.definition: The legal process of a court confirming that a dead person's will is valid and carrying out its instructions.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the final 't' a light, crisp sound. The vowel in the second syllable is the long 'ay' sound, not a reduced one.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a formal legal term that is often part of grief-related paperwork.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'probate' mainly in legal, financial and estate-planning contexts, and people often hear it when a relative dies. Lawyers may say 'the estate is in probate' to mean the court process has started. Casual speakers may not know the term, so explain it simply if needed.

distinctions.note: An estate is all the property a person owned; probate is the court process of settling that property.
A will is the document stating wishes; probate is the process of proving it valid.
A trust can often avoid probate, so people set one up to keep assets out of probate court.

examples.everyday: My aunt said the house will have to go through probate before we can sell it.
examples.professional: Our firm handles probate for estates under two million dollars, so we can file the paperwork this week.
examples.analytical: Probate functions as a public check on whether a testamentary instrument meets the legal requirements for validity.

nuance.analogy: Probate is like an official inspection stamp: the court checks the will and certifies that it is genuine before anyone acts on it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin probatum, 'proved,' from probare, 'to prove.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like 'probe' with a final 'd' sound; the final sound is 't'.
Confusing it with 'probable' or 'probation'.

probate.etymology: From Middle English *probate*, from Latin *probatus*, past participle of *probare* (“to test, examine, judge of”); see *probe*, *prove*.

senses.definition: Careless wastefulness.
Shameless and immoral behavior.

core.definition: Careless, extravagant wastefulness with money or resources; or shameless, immoral behavior.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, PROF-. The -ga- and final -cy are reduced, so the word ends with 'see' and not 'sy'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It signals strong disapproval of wasteful or immoral conduct.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use profligacy mainly in news commentary, political writing, and formal or literary discussion of government spending or moral decline. In everyday speech they would say 'wastefulness' or 'reckless spending'. Using it in casual conversation can sound stiff or pompous.

distinctions.note: Extravagance is spending lavishly on luxuries and can be neutral in tone; profligacy adds a stronger sense of irresponsibility.
Dissipation focuses on self-indulgent pleasure and moral decline; profligacy covers both reckless spending and immoral conduct.

examples.everyday: My uncle calls the new stadium project pure profligacy, and he is not shy about saying it.
examples.professional: The audit found profligacy in the department's cloud spending, with unused servers running for months.
examples.analytical: Critics of the regime described its fiscal profligacy as a moral failure as well as an economic one.

nuance.analogy: Profligacy is like a leaking bucket filled from a hose: the resources pour in and disappear faster than anyone can account for them.
nuance.etymology: From profligate, from Latin profligatus ('overthrown, ruined'), plus the suffix -acy.
common_mistakes: Confusing profligacy with profusion, which means abundance without the negative judgment.
Stressing the last syllables; the word has its main stress on PROF-.

profligacy.etymology: From *profligate* + *acy* (with -acy a suffixal construction from *-ate* + *-cy*), from Latin *prōflīgātus*, past participle of Latin *prōflīgō*, from *prō-* + *flīgō* (whence *pro-*).

senses.definition: A forefather, any of a person's direct ancestors.
A person from whom one or more people (dynasty, tribe, nation…) are descended.
senses.example: Abraham, alias Ibrahim, is the presumed progenitor of both the Jewish and Arab peoples.

senses.definition: A predecessor of something, especially if also a precursor or model.
senses.example: ARPANET was the progenitor of the Internet.

senses.definition: Someone who originates something.
A founder.
An ancestral form of a species.

core.definition: A forefather or direct ancestor; or a predecessor or model from which something later develops.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on -JEN-, with a hard j sound as in 'jet'. The final -tor is reduced to a rhotic 'ter', with the r clearly pronounced in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes origin without praise or blame.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use progenitor in history, biology, genealogy and technical writing, such as 'the progenitor of the programming language'. In everyday speech they would say 'ancestor', 'forefather' or 'the original'. Using it in casual talk can sound stiff, but it is natural in a formal discussion of origins.

distinctions.note: Ancestor is the everyday word for a relative from earlier generations; progenitor is more formal and can also mean an original model or source.
Precursor is a forerunner in time or development without necessarily being an ancestor; progenitor implies a direct line of descent or origin.

examples.everyday: My grandmother traced our family back to a single progenitor who arrived in 1850.
examples.professional: The first prototype is the progenitor of the entire microservices platform we run today.
examples.analytical: Aristotle is often regarded as the progenitor of formal logic in the Western tradition.

nuance.analogy: A progenitor is like the root of a tree: every branch and leaf comes from it, even though it is not visible in the top of the canopy.
nuance.etymology: From Latin progenitor, 'forefather', from progignere, 'to beget', with pro- ('forth') and gignere ('to beget').
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as PRO-genitor; the stress falls on -JEN-.
Confusing progenitor with progeny, which refers to offspring rather than the ancestor.

progenitor.etymology: From Middle English *progenitour*, from Anglo-Norman *progenitour*, Middle French *progeniteur* (Modern French *progéniteur*), and their etymon Latin *prōgenitor*, from *prōgenitus*, perfect participle of *prōgignō* (“to beget”), itself from *prō-*…

senses.definition: To predict or forecast, especially through the application of skill.
senses.example: Examining the tea-leaves, she prognosticated dark days ahead.

senses.definition: To presage, betoken.
senses.example: The bluebells may prognosticate an early spring this year.

core.definition: To predict or forecast the future, especially by using judgment, skill, or careful observation of signs.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on NAHS, the second syllable, and the vowel is the GA 'ah' of 'cot'. Don't pronounce the middle 'o' as 'oh'; it is 'ah'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly pretentious. It sounds learned, and in casual speech Americans prefer 'predict'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use prognosticate in writing, commentary, or deliberate formal speech, often for experts or pundits making forecasts, such as sports or political prognosticators. In everyday conversation people say 'predict' or 'guess'. It can sound stiff or showy if used simply to mean a casual guess.

distinctions.note: Predict is the everyday word; prognosticate is more formal and often implies relying on signs or expertise.
Foretell suggests knowing the future, often by supernatural means, while prognosticate suggests reasoned or expert forecasting.

examples.everyday: Everybody at the bar was prognosticating who would win the game tonight.
examples.professional: Our analysts prognosticate quarterly revenue, but their forecasts have been wrong for two years.
examples.analytical: Historians who prognosticate the collapse of empires often confuse pattern recognition with inevitability.

nuance.analogy: Like a weather vane reading the wind, a prognosticator reads present signs to point toward what comes next.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin prognosticare, 'to foretell', from Greek prognōstikos, 'knowing beforehand'.
common_mistakes: Using 'prognosticate' in casual speech where 'predict' is more natural.
Mispronouncing the second vowel as 'oh' instead of the GA 'ah' sound.

prognosticate.etymology: From Medieval Latin *prognosticare*; see *prognostic* for more.

senses.definition: To make known or make public.
To put into effect as a regulation.

core.definition: To announce or publish something officially, especially a law, rule or policy, so it becomes known and in effect.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable (PRAH-), and make the middle syllables short and reduced, as in 'mul'. Avoid stressing the -gate ending, which is a common error.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'promulgate' mainly in legal, governmental or academic writing, such as when an agency issues new regulations. In everyday speech, people say 'announce', 'issue', 'publish' or 'put into effect'. Using it in casual talk can sound stiff or pompous.

distinctions.note: Publish is general and everyday; promulgate implies official or formal announcement, often with legal force.
Announce is the everyday word for telling people something; promulgate suggests an authoritative act that makes a rule binding.

examples.everyday: The homeowners' association finally promulgated its new parking rules, and everyone complained about them.
examples.professional: The compliance team will promulgate the revised data-retention policy to all departments next week.
examples.analytical: Once the council promulgated the ordinance, it became binding on every district, regardless of local objections.

nuance.analogy: It is like posting a sign at the entrance of a park: once it is public, the rule applies to everyone who enters.
