nuance.etymology: From Latin promulgare, 'to make publicly known'.
common_mistakes: Using 'promulgate' for private or casual sharing; it implies an official announcement.
Stressing the last syllable as 'pro-mul-GATE'.

promulgate.etymology: Middle English *promulgaten*, from Latin *prōmulgātus*, of *prōmulgō* (“to make known, publish”), either from *provulgō* (“to make known, publish”), from *pro* (“forth”) + *vulgō* (“to publish”), or from *mulgeō* (“to bring forth”); see *-ate* and *-ate*.

senses.definition: Serving to instruct; didactic.
A didactic speech, book, etc.

core.definition: Intended to persuade or instruct someone, especially toward a way of life such as philosophy or virtue.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, and keep the final syllable short. The p is silent in the common English spelling pattern, but it is pronounced here as the first sound of the word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a purpose in writing or speech and carries no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use protreptic almost only in classical studies, philosophy and rhetoric. Ordinary speakers would say persuasive or instructive. It can describe a text meant to turn a reader toward a new way of living, such as an early philosophical dialogue.

distinctions.note: Persuasive is general and common, while protreptic specifically describes writing meant to convert a reader to a way of life, usually philosophy.
Didactic emphasizes teaching facts or morals, while protreptic emphasizes urging the reader to change how they live.

examples.everyday: My philosophy professor called that short essay protreptic, meaning it was written to convince us to study philosophy seriously.
examples.professional: The grant proposal read as a protreptic document, trying to persuade reviewers that the program mattered more than its budget.
examples.analytical: Aristotle's early dialogues are often read as protreptic works that aim to turn the reader toward the philosophical life.

nuance.analogy: A protreptic text is like a coach's pep talk, aimed at getting you to change your whole approach.
nuance.etymology: From Greek protreptikos, from protrepein (to turn forward, to exhort), from pro- (forward) and trepein (to turn).
common_mistakes: Using protreptic for any persuasive text, when the word has a specific meaning about turning someone toward a way of life.
Pronouncing the word as PRO-trep-tic with stress on the first syllable.

protreptic.etymology: Borrowed from Ancient Greek *προτρεπτικός* (“hortatory”), from *προτρέπω* (“to urge on”).

senses.definition: A sacred song; a poetical composition for use in the praise or worship of God.
One of the hymns by David and others, collected into one book of the Old Testament, or a modern metrical version of such a hymn for public worship.
To extol in psalms; to make music; to sing.
senses.example: to psalm his praises.

core.definition: A sacred song or poem of praise, prayer, or lament, especially one of the 150 in the biblical Book of Psalms.

pronunciation.tip: The 'l' and 'p' are silent: say SAHM, like 'Sam' with an open 'ah' vowel. Don't say 'sahlm' or 'p-sahm.'

nuance.connotation: Positive and reverent; associated with worship, comfort, and sometimes lament.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'a psalm' for one poem and 'Psalms' for the book, as in 'Psalm 23' or 'the Psalms.' It is common in church life, funerals, and Bible study. The verb sense is archaic.

distinctions.note: A hymn is a song of praise written for worship in any era, while a psalm is specifically from the biblical Psalms or modeled on them.
A canticle is a biblical song or hymn outside the Book of Psalms, such as the Magnificat.
A psalter is a book or collection of psalms.

examples.everyday: When my dad was in the hospital, I read Psalm 23 to him every night.
examples.professional: This morning's sermon will focus on Psalm 51 and what it teaches about repentance.
examples.analytical: The lament psalm typically moves from complaint to trust, a pattern that shapes how the community brings suffering before God.

nuance.analogy: A psalm is a prayer set to poetry, often meant to be sung.
nuance.etymology: From Old English psalm, from Latin psalmus, from Greek psalmos, 'song sung to a harp,' from psallein 'to pluck.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the 'p' or the 'l': say SAHM.
Writing 'Psalms 23' instead of 'Psalm 23' for a single psalm.
Using 'psalm' as an everyday verb.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew mizmor means 'a song with instrumental accompaniment,' and the book is called Tehillim, 'praises.' Psalm 23 speaks of the Lord as shepherd and gives comfort in the darkest valley. Psalm 51 is a prayer of repentance linked to David's sin with Bathsheba, and Psalm 150 closes the book with a call for everything that breathes to praise the Lord. Many psalms are attributed to David, as in 2 Samuel 23:1.

psalm.etymology: From Middle English *salm* or *psalme*, from Old English *psealm*, later reinforced from Old French *psalme* (modern French *psaume*), both from Latin *psalmus*, from Ancient Greek *ψαλμός* (“the sound emanating from twitching or twanging perhaps with the…

senses.definition: Initialism of parent-teacher organization.
Initialism of paid time off.
Initialism of power take-off, a powered shaft for driving auxiliary equipment.
Initialism of pick-to-order.
Initialism of please turn over (written at the end of the text on a page to say that it continues overleaf).

core.definition: Paid time off: the days employees can take as vacation, sick days or personal days while still receiving their normal pay.

pronunciation.tip: Say the letters P, T, and O, with the main stress on the final 'OH'. Each letter keeps its own short vowel sound, and the whole acronym is spoken as three letters.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use PTO constantly in workplace talk, especially in HR, emails and Slack. The phrase is often used in conversation, as in 'I have three days of PTO left.' Note that in the US PTO can cover vacation, sick days and personal days in one bank, so it is not the same as 'vacation.'

distinctions.note: Vacation is one kind of time off, while PTO is a pooled bank of days that may cover vacation, sick leave and personal days.
Sick leave is only for illness, while PTO can be used for many purposes depending on company policy.

examples.everyday: I'm using some of my PTO next week, so I'll be at the lake and not checking email.
examples.professional: Please submit your PTO request in the HR portal at least two weeks before the trip.
examples.analytical: Unlimited PTO policies may look generous, but they can discourage employees from taking any time off at all.

nuance.analogy: Like a shared bank account of days off that you draw from as life needs them.
nuance.etymology: An initialism of 'paid time off'.
common_mistakes: Using 'PTO' as a countable noun; say 'how much PTO' or 'a lot of PTO', not 'how many PTOs'.
Confusing PTO with 'vacation' in a US company, where the bank may include sick days.

conversation.text: I'm taking PTO next week, so Mike will cover for me.
How many PTO days do you have left this year?
She's on PTO until Monday, so let's wait for her input.

senses.definition: The bias to meta-analysis resulting from statistical studies with low statistical power tending to remain unpublished and inaccessible to the analyst.

core.definition: The tendency for studies with positive or significant results to be published more often than studies with null results, which distorts meta-analyses.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KAY in publication and on BY in bias, with the first syllable pub being a full vowel, not a schwa. Americans often link the two words so they sound like one rhythmic unit, pub-lih-KAY-shun-BY-us.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a technical term describing a methodological problem, sometimes presented as a warning about unreliable research.
nuance.usage_note: Used mainly by statisticians, epidemiologists, psychologists and researchers in evidence-based medicine when discussing meta-analysis and research integrity. In American academic talk it often comes up with the funnel plot and with the file drawer problem. Outside research circles, people say that studies are being selectively reported.

distinctions.note: The file drawer problem is the cause, meaning null studies are never submitted; publication bias is the resulting skew in the published literature.
Selection bias is a broader term for any non-random sampling of participants or data; publication bias is one specific type of selection affecting which studies get published.

collocations: a funnel plot to detect publication bias

examples.everyday: My friend who works in medicine said the new drug looks better than it really is because of publication bias.
examples.professional: Before we trust the pooled estimate, we should run a funnel plot and check for publication bias.
examples.analytical: Publication bias threatens the validity of meta-analysis because the published literature systematically overrepresents significant findings.

nuance.analogy: It is like judging a restaurant only by the reviews that get posted, while the disappointing visits never make it online.
nuance.etymology: Publication comes from Latin publicare, to make public; bias comes from French biais, slant.
common_mistakes: Saying 'publication bias' with stress on the wrong syllable, as in pub-li-CA-tion.
Using 'bias' as a verb with a preposition; the phrase is a fixed noun phrase, not 'biased for publication'.

senses.definition: To come to a stop, and turn off the road (i.e. onto the roadside or hard shoulder).
senses.example: Can you pull over just after the post office? My house is next door.

senses.definition: To command or force someone to drive their vehicle to the side of the road or curb and come to a stop.
senses.example: The cops pulled me over for speeding.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see pull,‎ over.

core.definition: Driven to the side of the road and stopped, often because a police officer signaled the driver to do so.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on OH in over, and pulled is a single syllable ending in a clear d sound. Do not add an extra vowel between the l and the d, and keep over lightly reduced to vur.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in ordinary driving talk, but it can sound stressful when it refers to a police stop.
nuance.usage_note: In American conversation, 'I got pulled over' almost always means a police officer stopped you. Drivers also say pull over when they need to stop safely to check a map or answer a phone. A natural reply to news of a stop is 'Oh no, did you get a ticket?'

distinctions.note: Pulled out means moving away from the curb or lane, often to drive forward, while pulled over means moving to the side and stopping.
Stopped is general, while pulled over suggests a deliberate move to the edge of the road, often under instruction.
Pulled up means arriving at or stopping near a place, not necessarily at the side of the road.

collocations: pulled over by a state trooper
pulled over to check the map

examples.everyday: I got pulled over on the way home for a broken taillight.
examples.professional: Our fleet driver was pulled over for a lane violation, so please send the dashcam footage to the safety team.
examples.analytical: Traffic stops often begin with a driver being pulled over for a minor infraction that can lead to a broader investigation.

nuance.analogy: Like a boat easing into the dock and tying up at the edge of the water.
common_mistakes: Using pulled over for stopping in the middle of the lane; it means stopping at the side of the road
Pronouncing pulled as two syllables

conversation.text: A cop pulled over the car in front of me for running a red light.
I was pulled over for having a broken taillight.
We saw a guy pulled over on the shoulder, changing a flat tire.

senses.definition: A type of four-dimensional hypercomplex number consisting of a real part and three imaginary parts (real multiples of distinct, independent square roots of −1 denoted by i, j and k); commonly used in vector mathematics and as an alternative to matrix algebra in calculating the rotation of three-dimensional objects.
A group or set of four people or things.
A word of four syllables.

core.definition: A four-part number in mathematics with one real part and three imaginary parts, used to describe 3D rotations.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, 'TUR', with the r-colored vowel. Many non-native speakers stress the first syllable or pronounce the final '-ion' as 'ee-ahn'; it is reduced to 'un' in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and purely technical.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'quaternion' almost only in mathematics, physics, computer graphics and robotics, typically when discussing rotations in three dimensions. Outside technical settings it is unfamiliar, and you may need to explain it. In software, engineers more often say 'quaternion' directly than describe the underlying algebra.

distinctions.note: A complex number has one real and one imaginary part; a quaternion has one real and three imaginary parts.
A matrix is a grid of numbers used for linear transformations; a quaternion is a compact four-number way to represent rotation, avoiding some matrix issues.
A vector is a list of numbers with magnitude and direction; a quaternion extends this idea with an extra real component.

collocations: represent a rotation as a quaternion

examples.everyday: My cousin who builds drones said their control software uses quaternions so the camera doesn't wobble.
examples.professional: We switched the robot arm's orientation code to quaternions, which avoids the gimbal lock we saw with Euler angles.
examples.analytical: Hamilton's discovery of quaternions in 1843 showed that a non-commutative algebra could describe rotations in three-dimensional space.

nuance.analogy: A quaternion is like a compact remote control for turning an object in space: four numbers give you a smooth turn without the clumsy buttons of a matrix.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin 'quaternio' (a group of four), from Latin 'quattuor' (four).
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as KWAT-er-nee-un instead of kwuh-TUR-nee-un.
Confusing it with 'quaternary' (a group of four or a geologic period).

quaternion.etymology: From Middle English *quaterniǒun*, from Late Latin *quaterniō*, from *quaternus* (“four each”) + *-iō*, from *quater* (“four times”).

senses.definition: A thing that is the most perfect example of its type; the most perfect embodiment of something; epitome, prototype.
A pure substance.
senses.example: (Can we add an example for this sense?)

senses.definition: The essence of a thing in its purest and most concentrated form.
The fifth alchemical element, or essence, after earth, air, fire, and water that fills the universe beyond the terrestrial sphere.
A hypothetical form of dark energy postulated to explain observations of an accelerating universe.
To reduce to its purest and most concentrated essence.

core.definition: The purest and most concentrated form of something; the perfect example or embodiment of a quality.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, TES. The first syllable is 'kwin', not 'kwen', and the last two syllables are reduced, so the word ends with 'uns'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises something as the purest, most complete example of its kind.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use quintessence in formal writing, reviews, essays and speeches to praise something as the perfect example of its type. In casual speech they would say the best example, the epitome or the very definition of. It fits well in a toast or a tribute.

distinctions.note: Essence is the basic nature of a thing; quintessence is its purest, most concentrated form.
Epitome is a common word for the perfect example; quintessence is more formal and emphasizes purity and concentration.

examples.everyday: At the wedding toast, my brother said she was the quintessence of kindness.
examples.professional: The design review focused on the quintessence of the product: fast, simple and reliable.
examples.analytical: For Aquinas, the quintessence of the moral law is love, which orders all other virtues toward God.

nuance.analogy: Quintessence is like a shot of espresso: the strong, concentrated core of something that was once a larger brew.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin quinta essentia, 'fifth essence', the substance believed to make up the heavens, beyond the four elements.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (KWIN-tuh-sens) instead of the second.
Using quintessence for an everyday small thing; it suggests the purest and most perfect form.

quintessence.etymology: From Middle English, borrowed from Middle French, from Medieval Latin *quinta essentia* (“fifth essence, aether”), equivalent to *quint-* + *essence*.

senses.definition: A fragment of a human expression that is repeated by somebody else, for example from literature or a famous speech.
senses.example: "Where they burn books, they will also burn people" is a famous quotation from Heinrich Heine.

senses.definition: The act of quoting someone or something.
A price that has been quoted for buying or selling.
senses.example: Let's get a quotation for repairing the roof before we decide whether it's worth doing.

senses.definition: The act of setting a price.

core.definition: A passage or phrase repeated word for word from a book, speech, or another person, often to support an argument.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, TAY. The final syllable is a reduced, nearly silent "-tion" that Americans say as "shun," so avoid adding a full extra vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is positive or neutral in academic and professional settings, where quoting a source shows credibility.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use quotation mostly for words repeated from a text or speaker, and they often shorten it to "quote" in speech. In casual talk, "quote" as a noun is common ("Give me a good quote"), but "quotation" is more formal and appears in writing, style guides, and academic work. The term also covers the act of quoting a price in business, though "quote" is more common for that sense.

distinctions.note: Quote is the everyday, shorter form used in speech and informal writing; quotation is more formal and common in academic writing.
A quotation is the repeated words themselves, while a citation is the reference that identifies where those words came from.

examples.everyday: My dad always has a favorite quotation from Mark Twain for every situation.
examples.professional: Please add a quotation from the client's survey to the slide so the finding has a source.
examples.analytical: The author's use of a single quotation from Augustine carries more weight than the paragraphs of paraphrase surrounding it.

nuance.analogy: A quotation is like a photograph of someone's words: it captures them exactly as they were spoken or written, frozen in a new setting.
nuance.etymology: From Latin quotare, "to mark with numbers," from quot, "how many."
common_mistakes: Saying "quotation" for a casual one-line saying; "quote" is more natural in speech.
Stressing the wrong syllable as KWO-tay-shun; the main stress is on TAY.

quotation.etymology: The obsolete sense of, from Medieval Latin *quotātiō*, from Latin *quotō*, is attested from the 15th century.

senses.definition: Harsh and rough-sounding.
senses.example: At night, raucous ruckus took place in the swamp.

senses.definition: Disorderly and boisterous.
senses.example: Acts of vandalism were committed by a raucous gang of drunkards.

senses.definition: Loud and annoying.
senses.example: The new neighbors had a raucous ruction in the small hours last night.

core.definition: Loud, harsh, and rough-sounding, especially in a noisy or disorderly way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a weak schwa, so say RAW-kus with no strong second vowel. Keep the r clear, and do not pronounce the -ous as a full separate syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes noise or behavior that is harsh or out of control.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use raucous in writing, news reports, and descriptions of crowds, parties, or birds. In casual talk, people more often say loud, noisy, or rowdy. Raucous is stronger than loud, so it fits a bar full of shouting fans better than a quiet concert.

distinctions.note: Loud describes volume; raucous adds a harsh, rough, and disorderly quality.
Rowdy describes rough, disorderly behavior; raucous describes the harsh, noisy sound of that behavior.

examples.everyday: The bar got really raucous after the game, so we left early.
examples.professional: The raucous debate in the planning meeting made it hard to hear the customer's concerns.
examples.analytical: Dickens uses raucous street scenes to show the disorder of the city beneath its polished surface.

nuance.analogy: Raucous sound is like a rusty gate that screeches every time someone pushes it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin raucus, hoarse or harsh-sounding.
common_mistakes: Using raucous for a pleasant loud sound, such as a cheerful bird song.
Pronouncing it as ROW-kus instead of RAW-kus.

senses.definition: Voracious and greedy.
senses.example: There is no shortage of ravening friends and relatives on the day one hits the lottery.

senses.definition: Eagerness for plunder; rapacity; extortion.

core.definition: Very hungry, greedy, and aggressive in seeking food, prey, or gain.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the middle syllable is a weak schwa, so say RAV-uh-ning. The -ing ending should be short and light, not a long ee sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative; suggests fierce, uncontrolled hunger or greed.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ravening mainly in literature, sermons, and poetic descriptions of predators or greedy people. It is strong and dramatic, so do not use it for someone who simply wants lunch. For everyday speech, use hungry, starving, or ravenous instead.

distinctions.note: Ravenous is the common everyday word for very hungry; ravening is more literary and suggests predatory greed.
Greedy is a plain judgment of wanting too much; ravening adds the image of a wild hunting animal.

examples.everyday: After the hike, the kids came in with ravening appetites and ate everything in the fridge.
examples.professional: The investor was described by the press as ravening for control of the market, which made the board nervous.
examples.analytical: The prophet's image of ravening wolves exposes leaders who exploit the flock rather than feed it.

nuance.analogy: A ravening animal is like a hungry wolf that sees the flock as food rather than family.
nuance.etymology: From raven, to seize greedily, from Old French ravir, to seize.
common_mistakes: Using ravening for ordinary hunger instead of ravenous.
Confusing ravening with raven, the noun for the bird.

ravening.etymology: Present participle of the obsolete verb *raven* (“to prey”).

senses.definition: To exchange two things, with both parties giving one thing and taking another thing.
To give something else in response (where the "thing" may also be abstract, a feeling or action) To make a reciprocal gift.
senses.example: I gave them apples from my tree; they reciprocated with a pie and some apple jelly.

senses.definition: To move backwards and forwards, like a piston.
senses.example: a reciprocating engine

senses.definition: To counter, retort or retaliate.

core.definition: To give or do something back in return for what someone has given or done for you.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on SIP, and the first syllable is reduced to a weak 'rih'. The 'pr' cluster is quick, and the final 't' is a clear, light American 't' before a pause.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes fair, mutual giving, though it can sound stiff in casual talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use reciprocate mostly in polite, formal, or written contexts, such as thanking a host or answering a formal invitation. In everyday speech they more often say 'return the favor' or 'pay it back'. A natural reply to a kind gesture is a simple 'Thank you, I'll do the same for you sometime.'

distinctions.note: Return is broader and more everyday; reciprocate stresses matching a gift, kindness, or feeling with one of similar value.
Retaliate means to strike back in anger or hostility, while reciprocate is neutral or friendly.

examples.everyday: My neighbor brought us a casserole when we were sick, so I want to reciprocate with a pie.
examples.professional: Our partner shared their customer data with us, so we'll reciprocate by sending them the full test results next week.
examples.analytical: A covenant of trust holds only when each party is willing to reciprocate the commitments the other has made.

nuance.analogy: Like passing a ball back and forth: each throw is answered by a throw in return.
nuance.etymology: From Latin reciprocare, 'to move back and forth', from reciprocus, 'moving back and forth'.
common_mistakes: Using reciprocate for 'accept' or 'receive' without giving something back, as in 'I reciprocate the gift' when you only thanked someone.
Saying 'reciprocate to' instead of 'reciprocate with' or using it directly with the object.

reciprocate.etymology: From Latin *recīprocātus*, perfect passive participle of *recīprocō* (“to move back and forth”) (see *-ate*), from *reciprocus* + *-ō*, itself possibly from a phrase such as *reque proque* (“back and forth”), from *re-* (“back”), *prō* (“forwards”) and…

senses.definition: A starting or falling back; a rebound; a shrinking.
senses.example: the recoil of nature, or of the blood

senses.definition: The state or condition of having recoiled.
The energy transmitted back to the shooter from a firearm which has fired. Recoil is a function of the weight of the weapon, the weight of the projectile, and the speed at which it leaves the muzzle.
An escapement in which, after each beat, the scape-wheel recoils slightly.
To pull back, especially in disgust, horror or astonishment.
senses.example: He recoiled in disgust when he saw the mess.

senses.definition: Of a firearm: to quickly push back when fired.

core.definition: To jerk or spring back, especially in disgust, fear or surprise; also, a gun kicking back when fired.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable and pronounce the diphthong 'oy' clearly as in 'coil'. Learners often shorten the vowel, so keep it long and smooth.

nuance.connotation: Negative or strong. It usually signals disgust, fear or shock, though in firearms it is a neutral technical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'recoil' for a sudden, strong physical or emotional pulling back, such as 'I recoiled at the smell.' Hunters and shooters use it for the kick of a gun. In everyday talk, 'flinch' or 'pull back' may be more natural for small reactions.

distinctions.note: Flinch is a quick, involuntary movement, while recoil can be more deliberate or emotional and often suggests disgust.
Retreat is a planned withdrawal, usually from a place or position, while recoil is an instinctive pullback.

examples.everyday: I recoiled when the waiter said the fish was still raw in the middle.
examples.professional: Several team members recoiled at the idea of rewriting the whole pipeline before the launch.
examples.analytical: Many readers recoil from the author's argument because it seems to justify the violence it describes.

nuance.analogy: Like a spring pressed down that snaps back, a person who recoils springs away from something that shocks them.
nuance.etymology: From Old French reculer, to go backward, from Latin re- back and culus, the rear.
common_mistakes: Using 'recoil' for ordinary walking backward; it implies a stronger reaction.
Confusing it with 'recall', which is a memory or a call back.

senses.definition: To refuse to accept; to forswear.
senses.example: She even rejected my improved offer.

senses.definition: To block a shot, especially if it sends the ball off the court.
To refuse a romantic advance.
senses.example: I've been rejected three times this week.

senses.definition: Something that is rejected.
An unpopular person.
A rejected defective product in a production line.
A rejected takeoff.

core.definition: To refuse to accept something, or to refuse to give someone what they ask for or hope for.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, -JECT, and the first syllable is a short, reduced vowel. Do not stress the first syllable as you would in the noun REJ-ect used in some other contexts, and keep the j sound clear.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral. Rejecting an offer, a person or an idea is usually unpleasant for the one who receives it, but the word itself is plain and neutral in most contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use reject for job applications, proposals, offers and ideas, as in 'They rejected our offer.' In casual speech people often say 'turn down' for offers and invitations, which sounds friendlier. For products, reject is common in manufacturing and quality control, and as a noun, a reject is a defective item.

distinctions.note: Decline is softer and more polite, often used for invitations or offers you politely do not accept, while reject sounds more definite and can feel harsh.
Refuse emphasizes an active unwillingness to do or accept something, and it often describes a direct, sometimes stubborn, choice; reject implies judging something and turning it away.
Deny means to state that something is not true or not granted, while reject means to turn away or not accept something that was offered or proposed.

examples.everyday: My landlord rejected my first rental application, so I had to look at other apartments.
examples.professional: The review board rejected our proposal because the budget was not justified in enough detail.
examples.analytical: Locke's critics reject the claim that the mind begins as a blank slate, arguing that certain innate capacities precede experience.

nuance.analogy: Think of a bouncer at a club door who looks at your ID and sends you back into the street; that is what it means to reject someone or something.
nuance.etymology: From Latin reicere, meaning to throw back, from re- (back) and iacere (to throw).
common_mistakes: Using reject with a preposition, as in 'reject to the offer'; say 'reject the offer' with no preposition.
Stressing the first syllable (RE-ject) as in the noun, which is a different pronunciation pattern from the verb.

reject.etymology: From Late Middle English *rejecten*, from Latin *reiectus*, past participle of *reicio* (“to throw back”), from *re-* (“back”) + *iacio* (“to throw”).

senses.definition: An interpretation or performance of an artwork, especially a musical score or musical work.
A given visual reproduction of something.
Translation between languages, or between forms of a language; a translated text or work.
Formal deliverance of a verdict.
The handing-over of someone wanted for justice who has fled a given jurisdiction.
(rare) The surrender (of a city, fortress etc.).
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: (rare) The handing over of a person or thing.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: To surrender or hand over (a person or thing); especially, for one jurisdiction to do so to another.

core.definition: An artistic performance or interpretation of a piece of music, a play, or a song, or a particular version of it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, 'DISH'. The final syllable is a reduced schwa, so it sounds like 'un'. Don't pronounce the d as a hard sound followed by a separate syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It implies a skillful or personal interpretation of an existing work.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use rendition in music, theater, and art reviews, as in 'her rendition of the national anthem'. In everyday talk, version is more common. Rendition sounds elevated in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Version is the everyday, neutral word for any variant of a work; rendition emphasizes the performer's interpretation.
Rendering can be a technical output or a translation; rendition is mainly used for performances and artistic interpretations.

examples.everyday: Did you hear her rendition of that old Dolly Parton song at the wedding?
examples.professional: Our marketing video features a fresh rendition of the company jingle for the holiday campaign.
examples.analytical: Each critic's rendition of the Hamlet soliloquy reveals a different reading of the character's doubt.

nuance.analogy: A rendition is like a cover of a song: the notes are the same, but the performer's choices give it a new shape.
nuance.etymology: From render, from Latin reddere, meaning to give back or to deliver, with the sense of interpreting a work.
common_mistakes: Using rendition to mean a translation of a text, when translation is more usual in American English.
Stressing the first syllable, as in REN-di-shun.

rendition.etymology: From obsolete French *rendition*, alteration (after *rendre* (“to render”)) of *reddition* (“reddition”).

senses.definition: Answering, replying or responding.
Able to receive and respond to external stimuli.
Using antiphons; antiphonal.
Susceptible to the feelings of others.
Automatically resizing and repositioning elements to fit the available space.

core.definition: Quick to react helpfully to people's requests, questions or needs; quick to respond.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on SPAHN, and the -sive ending is a weak syllable, so say it as 'siv', not 'sive'. The s in the middle is voiceless.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises quickness and attentiveness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'responsive' for people who answer promptly, such as 'Our team is very responsive' or 'the doctor's office is responsive'. In tech, 'responsive design' means a website adjusts to different screen sizes. In casual speech, 'quick to reply' or 'gets back to you fast' is also common.

distinctions.note: 'Responsible' means accountable or in charge; 'responsive' means reacting quickly to people or events.
'Reactive' often implies responding only after a problem appears; 'responsive' suggests a positive, attentive willingness to help.

examples.everyday: My landlord is really responsive, so whenever something breaks, he fixes it within a day.
examples.professional: Our support team has to stay responsive to customer tickets during the holiday launch.
examples.analytical: A responsive ethics attends to the particular needs of the people affected, not only to abstract rules.

nuance.analogy: Like a good dog that comes the moment you call: quick, attentive and ready to act.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin responsivus, from respondere, 'to answer'.
common_mistakes: Using 'responsive to' with the wrong preposition; say 'responsive to' a need or request.
Confusing 'responsive' with 'responsible'; they look alike but mean different things.

responsive.etymology: From Middle French *responsif*, from Late Latin *responsivus*.

senses.definition: Vengeful, vindictive.

core.definition: Wanting revenge; inclined to punish someone for harm done to you.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable 'VENJ.' The 'g' before 'e' sounds like a 'j,' and the final '-ful' is a reduced syllable, not a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative; suggests a bitter or unforgiving desire for payback.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use revengeful to describe a person's mood or behavior, often in fiction or ordinary conversation about conflict. Vengeful is more common in formal writing, and vindictive is stronger and more clinical. Calling someone revengeful can sound harsh in conversation.

distinctions.note: Vengeful and revengeful are close in meaning; vengeful is more common and slightly more formal in American usage.
Vindictive is stronger and implies deliberate, spiteful punishment; revengeful is more general.

examples.everyday: After the breakup, she felt revengeful, but she eventually let it go.
examples.professional: A revengeful response to the complaint would only make the dispute worse.
examples.analytical: The tragedy shows how a revengeful heart destroys the very justice it claims to seek.

nuance.analogy: A revengeful mood is like a coal that stays hot long after the fire is out.
nuance.etymology: From revenge (from Old French revenger, to avenge) plus the suffix -ful.
common_mistakes: Using 'revengeful' as a synonym for 'revenge' (the noun), as in 'a revengeful plan.'
Mispronouncing the 'g' in 'revenge' as a hard 'g.'

senses.definition: Special equipment or gear used for a particular purpose.
senses.example: The climbers each had a different rig for climbing that particular rockface.

senses.definition: A large truck, especially a semi-trailer truck.
senses.example: Every rig at the truckstop had custom-made mud-flaps.

senses.definition: The special apparatus used for drilling wells.
A costume or an outfit.
senses.example: My sister and I always made our own rigs for Halloween.

senses.definition: A personal computer, typically one modified for looks.
An imperfectly castrated horse, sheep etc.
Radio equipment, especially a citizen's band transceiver.
Equipment used for taking recreational drugs.
A model outfitted with parameterized controls for animation.
A promiscuous woman.
An algebraic structure similar to a ring, but without the requirement that every element have an additive inverse.
The rigging of a sailing ship or other such craft.
To fit out with a harness or other equipment.
senses.example: To rig such massive equipment requires experienced riggers

senses.definition: To move (a heavy object) with the help of slings, hoists, block and tackle, levers, or similar equipment.
senses.example: To rig such massive equipment requires experienced riggers

senses.definition: To dress or clothe in some costume.
To make or construct something in haste or in a makeshift manner.
senses.example: rig up a makeshift shelter

senses.definition: To manipulate something dishonestly for personal gain or discriminatory purposes.
senses.example: to rig an election

senses.definition: To outfit a model with controls for animation.
To equip and fit (a ship) with sails, shrouds, and yards.

core.definition: Special equipment or gear set up together for a particular job, such as an oil drilling rig.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a short i and a hard g at the end. Do not add a vowel after the g.

nuance.connotation: Neutral as equipment; negative when it means fixing a result dishonestly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use rig for oil drilling rigs, big rigs (large semi trucks), and camera or sound setups: 'Our camera rig is ready.' Informally, rig or rigged can mean an election or game was fixed, so context matters.

distinctions.note: Gear is general equipment; a rig suggests a set of items assembled together for one purpose.
Equipment is formal and general; rig is more specific and informal.

examples.everyday: The truck driver pulled his big rig into the lot next to the diner.
examples.professional: Let's test the new camera rig before the client walks in.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that the procedure rigs the outcome in favor of incumbents, whatever the stated rules.

nuance.analogy: A rig is like a kit: all the parts assembled ready for one job.
nuance.etymology: Middle English riggen, to fit out a ship with rigging; the exact origin is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Confusing rig with rigor; they are different words with different meanings.
Assuming rig always means a truck; in oil or sound work it means a setup of equipment.

rig.etymology: From Early Modern English *rygge*, probably of origin.

senses.definition: The quality of being rotten.

core.definition: The state or quality of being rotten, either physically decayed or morally corrupt.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, RAHT. The -en- is a syllabic n, so there is no clear vowel before the second n. The final -ness is a reduced 'nus'.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. It describes decay or corruption and is more serious than casual uses of 'rotten'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use rottenness in everyday speech; they usually say 'rot' or 'the rotten part'. It appears in sermons, essays, and literary writing about moral corruption. In casual talk, 'the rot' is more natural.

distinctions.note: Rot is the everyday noun for decay, while rottenness is more abstract and literary.
Corruption often means dishonesty by officials, while rottenness can describe a general state of decay or moral decline.

examples.everyday: The house looked fine from the street, but the rottenness in the porch was obvious when we stepped on it.
examples.professional: The audit uncovered a rottenness in the accounting process that had been hidden for years.
examples.analytical: Paul's warnings about the rottenness of the flesh and the corruption of desire invite careful reading of Romans 8 and Galatians 5.

nuance.analogy: Rottenness is like a hidden crack in a beam: the building stands until the weight shows what has been eating it away.
nuance.etymology: From rotten and the suffix -ness, meaning the state of being.
common_mistakes: Using it as a casual everyday word; 'rot' or 'the rotten part' is more natural in speech.
Confusing it with 'rotundness', which describes a round body shape.
nuance.biblical_note: Proverbs 12:4 uses the image of rottenness in the bones to describe a disgraceful wife who brings shame to her husband, and Proverbs 14:30 says passion makes the bones rot, contrasting it with a tranquil mind. In these passages the bones stand for the inner strength or health of a person, so rottenness points to inner decay rather than only outward failure.

core.definition: The Greek transliteration of an Aramaic phrase meaning 'you have forsaken me', spoken by Jesus on the cross.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, 'BAHK'. The 'th' is unvoiced, as in 'thin', and the final syllable is a light 'nee'.

nuance.connotation: Solemn and religious; a serious phrase used in sermons and Bible study.
nuance.usage_note: In American churches this word appears in the Gospel accounts and is usually explained in sermons rather than used in everyday speech. Most people refer to it as the cry of dereliction or as the question Jesus asks on the cross. It is not a word you would use in casual conversation.

examples.everyday: At church, the pastor read the words from the cross, including the cry that begins with sabachthani.
examples.professional: In the Good Friday service, the choir sings a setting of the words Jesus spoke, including the Aramaic phrase sabachthani.
examples.analytical: The Greek sabachthani transliterates Aramaic and preserves the cry of Psalm 22:1, which shapes the Gospel writers' presentation of Jesus' suffering.

nuance.analogy: Sabachthani is like a heartfelt cry in a foreign language, carrying its full weight even for those who don't speak it.
nuance.etymology: Greek transliteration of an Aramaic phrase, rendered in the Gospels.
common_mistakes: Mistaking it for an ordinary word or a name; it is a Gospel transliteration.
Putting the stress on the final syllable instead of the second one.
nuance.biblical_note: The word appears in Matthew 27:46 and Mark 15:34, where Jesus cries out in Aramaic from the cross, and the Gospel writers record it in Greek letters. The Aramaic phrase means 'you have forsaken me' and echoes the opening words of Psalm 22:1 in Hebrew. Matthew and Mark both report the cry, showing Jesus experiencing abandonment and suffering while still speaking the words of Scripture.

senses.definition: Yellowish.
Of an unhealthy pale color.
Of a tan color, associated with people from southern Europe or East Asia.
Having skin (especially on the face) of a sickly pale color.
Having a similar pale, yellowish color.
Foul; murky; sickly.
To become sallow.
To cause (someone or something) to become sallow.
A European willow, Salix caprea, that has broad leaves, large catkins and tough wood.
A willow twig or branch.

core.definition: Having an unhealthy, yellowish or pale complexion, often looking tired or sick.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SAL. The second syllable is a long o, so say it as SAL-oh, not SAL-ow as in cow.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a sick or tired appearance and can sound unkind if said about a person directly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sallow mainly in literary writing or descriptive prose, such as 'his sallow face after the long illness.' In conversation, people say 'pale,' 'sickly' or 'yellowish' instead. Calling a friend sallow in speech could sound harsh, so use it carefully.

distinctions.note: Pale is common and can be neutral, while sallow specifically suggests a yellowish, unhealthy tint.
Wan describes weakness or exhaustion in a pale face, while sallow emphasizes the yellow color.

examples.everyday: Honey, you look a little sallow; maybe you should get some sleep.
examples.professional: Her sallow complexion after the flu was noticeable, so I asked if she needed to go home.
examples.analytical: The novelist uses sallow skin as an image of moral decay, linking the body's appearance to the character's inner state.

nuance.analogy: Sallow is like an old newspaper left in the sun: a yellowed color that suggests age or neglect.
nuance.etymology: From Old English 'salu', dusky or dark, which came to mean yellowish.
common_mistakes: Using sallow to mean 'shallow'; the words are unrelated.
Pronouncing the final syllable as ow as in cow, when it is oh.

sallow.etymology: From Middle English *salowe*, from Old English *salu*, from **salu*, from Proto-Germanic **salwaz*, from Proto-Indo-European **selH-*.

core.definition: The first king of ancient Israel, chosen by the prophet Samuel, who later persecuted Christians before becoming the apostle Paul.

pronunciation.tip: Pronounce it as one syllable with the 'aw' vowel of 'caught'. It rhymes with 'all' and 'call' rather than 'soul'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It names a biblical figure and is respectful in religious contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Saul mainly in Bible study, church, or history conversations. In Scripture, the name appears as Saul until Acts 13, where the narrative refers to him as Paul. Ordinary friends may mention him when discussing the conversion story.

distinctions.note: Paul is the name used for the same man after his conversion and in most of the New Testament letters, while Saul is his earlier Jewish name.

collocations: Saul on the road to Damascus

examples.everyday: At Bible study last night, we talked about how Saul went from King Saul to the apostle Paul.
examples.professional: In my sermon series on Acts, I'll explain why Saul's name changes in the narrative.
examples.analytical: The narrative of Saul's kingship in 1 Samuel contrasts sharply with the later story of Saul of Tarsus, whose transformation reframes the older account of divine election.

nuance.analogy: Saul is like a man whose story has two chapters under two names: the first king, then the apostle Paul.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Shaʾul, meaning asked for or requested.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like 'soul', which is a different word.
Confusing King Saul with Saul of Tarsus, who later became Paul; they are the same name in different periods of the story.
nuance.biblical_note: Saul is the first king of Israel, from the tribe of Benjamin, chosen when the people asked for a king. The Hebrew name Shaʾul means asked for or requested. 1 Samuel 10:1 describes Samuel anointing him as king. 1 Samuel 15:26 says the LORD rejected him from being king after he disobeyed.

senses.definition: In a serious or literal manner.
senses.example: He was hoping that we would take him seriously.

senses.definition: Used to attempt to introduce a serious point in a less serious conversation.
senses.example: Now, seriously, why did you forget to feed the cat today?

senses.definition: Gravely; deeply; very much.
senses.example: That was a seriously unpleasant thing to say.

senses.definition: Used to call back to a previous point, in disbelief or for emphasis.
senses.example: You baked ten (10) cakes. Seriously, why did you do that?

senses.definition: In an extreme or major way; majorly.
senses.example: Unless you're seriously strapped (armed), you're about to be not okay too.

core.definition: In a serious way, in earnest; also used to show you are not joking or to stress how strongly you mean something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SEER, and the middle syllable is weak, so it sounds like 'SEER-ee-us-lee' with two quick syllables. Americans often run 'us' and 'lee' together, sounding like 'SEER-ee-slee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly emphatic. It can show sincerity, shock, or annoyance depending on tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say 'Seriously?' or 'Are you serious?' in casual talk to react with surprise or disbelief. As a sentence starter, 'Seriously, though...' shifts a joking talk to a real point. It can sound sarcastic if the tone is flat, so use it carefully in meetings.

distinctions.note: Really is the most common all-purpose intensifier; seriously is more emphatic and often expresses disbelief or strong feeling.
Truly sounds sincere and formal; seriously sounds casual and direct.

examples.everyday: Seriously, you tried that new taco place? How was it?
examples.professional: Seriously, we need to fix the flaky tests before we merge this branch.
examples.analytical: If we seriously consider the ethics of this model, we cannot ignore the bias in the training data.

nuance.analogy: It works like a volume knob that turns up the meaning, making a sentence sound more sincere or more shocked.
nuance.etymology: From serious, from Latin seriosus, from serius, earnest, plus the adverb ending -ly.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle syllable too strongly, making it 'seer-ee-us-lee' with three equal beats.
Using it as a sentence for every doubt; too many 'seriously?' replies can sound dismissive.

conversation.text: "I'm moving to Paris." "Seriously? When?"
Seriously? Someone took my parking spot again?
I'm seriously thinking about getting a dog.

core.definition: The Hebrew form of the name Saul, the first king of Israel, and in Acts also the name of Paul before his conversion.

pronunciation.tip: Say it as one stressed syllable, with the American "ah" vowel of "hot" in the cot-caught merger, so it sounds like "SHAHL". Do not add an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a name used in scholarship and religious studies rather than daily life.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say Saul in everyday speech and in most English Bibles, including the RSV. Shaul is the transliteration used in Jewish and scholarly contexts, so you might see it in academic writing or Hebrew Bible study. Using Shaul in casual talk may sound unusually formal.

distinctions.note: Saul is the standard English form used in the RSV, while Shaul shows the Hebrew transliteration.

examples.everyday: In Sunday school we talked about Shaul, the first king, and how he struggled with jealousy.
examples.professional: In my commentary on Samuel I refer to the king as Shaul to match the Hebrew text.
examples.analytical: The narrative of Shaul's anointing in 1 Samuel 10:1 raises questions about the relation between prophetic designation and royal legitimacy.

nuance.analogy: Like hearing a name in its original language and recognizing the familiar person behind it.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Šā'ûl, meaning "asked for" or "requested".
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as "shah-OOL", with stress on the second syllable.
Mixing it with the English word "shawl", which is spelled differently and means a wrap.
nuance.biblical_note: In Hebrew the name is Šā'ûl, meaning asked for, and it is the same name as Saul in English Bibles. 1 Samuel 9:2 describes Saul son of Kish as a tall, handsome man. 1 Samuel 10:1 says that Samuel anointed Saul to be prince over Israel. Acts 13:9 notes that Saul was also called Paul, linking the two names in the New Testament.

core.definition: A son of Judah and an ancestor of a family line in Israel, and also a grandson of Shem in Genesis, whose name is used for several family groups.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final vowel is a reduced schwa. Speakers sometimes pronounce the second syllable as a full long vowel, but it should be quiet.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Used in Bible study and genealogy discussions. Americans say SHEE-luh, and the name appears in Genesis, Numbers and Chronicles. It is not used as a common English word.

examples.everyday: I was reading Genesis and got confused, because there is a Shelah who is Judah's son and another one in the family tree.
examples.professional: In the genealogy table, I list Shelah under Judah with the clans that came from him.
examples.analytical: The repeated name Shelah in Genesis 10 and Genesis 38 shows how the biblical genealogies link different branches under a shared family name.

nuance.analogy: Like a family name that shows up in two branches of the same family tree, each time marking a different line.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Shelah, possibly meaning 'sending' or 'petition' (uncertain).
common_mistakes: Confusing Shelah with Shiloh, a place where the tabernacle stood.
Pronouncing the second syllable as a full vowel.
nuance.biblical_note: Shelah appears as a son of Judah in Genesis 38:5, 11, 14 and 26, where Judah's sons and their relations to Tamar are recounted. Genesis 10:24 and 11:12-15 name a different Shelah, the son of Arphaxad and father of Eber, in the line of Shem. Numbers 26:20 lists the clan of Shelah among the families of Judah. These passages show how the name marks different family lines in the biblical genealogies.

senses.definition: Send a quick text message (casual).

core.definition: To quickly send a short text message to someone on a phone.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'text,' and 'a' is reduced to a quick schwa. In fast speech it sounds like 'shoo-duh TEKST,' with the t in 'text' often unreleased.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and casual. It is friendly and brief, suited to everyday contact with friends, family, and colleagues you know well.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'shoot me a text' or 'I'll shoot you a text' when they plan to message someone quickly. A natural reply is 'Sounds good' or 'Will do.' In work settings, 'send me an email' or 'ping me' may be more appropriate, and 'shoot a text' is generally for personal or casual contact.

distinctions.note: 'Text' alone is the everyday verb; 'shoot a text' adds a casual, quick tone.
'Call' means phoning and speaking live, while 'shoot a text' means sending a written message.

collocations: shoot a text to the group

examples.everyday: I'll shoot you a text when I'm on my way.
examples.professional: I'll shoot you a text once the meeting room is confirmed.
examples.analytical: Informal messaging norms, such as shooting a text instead of formally writing, shape how teams coordinate.

nuance.analogy: Like firing off a quick arrow of a message that lands instantly.
nuance.etymology: 'Shoot' from Old English 'scēotan,' meaning to propel or discharge, extended to quick sending.
common_mistakes: Saying 'send a text me' instead of 'shoot me a text' or 'send me a text.'
Stressing 'shoot' instead of 'text.'

conversation.text: Shoot me a text when you're outside.
I'll shoot a text to the team about the change.
He shot me a text saying he's running late.

senses.definition: To close, terminate, or end; to stop operating, either permanently or temporarily.
senses.example: The store was shut down at the end of the year.

senses.definition: To turn off or stop.
senses.example: It's a good idea to shut down the machine before you leave.

senses.definition: To stop offering a service, such as a bar; to perform the necessary tasks to stop a service or close a function.
senses.example: The restaurant shuts down at two o'clock in the morning.

senses.definition: To suppress, block out, or reject something.
senses.example: She made a proposal to reorganize the department, but management shut her down.

senses.definition: To pass (another vehicle), especially quickly.
senses.example: I opened that throttle and shut him down.

senses.definition: To render (something) ineffective.
senses.example: We shut down the other team's strategy.

senses.definition: To emotionally withdraw into oneself as a defense mechanism; to block out external stressors.
senses.example: I can't talk to him about the accident; he just shuts down anytime I try.

senses.definition: (dated) To become dark.
senses.example: Once the night shut down, I couldn't see my way home.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: To close a business, system, or device so it stops operating, either temporarily or permanently.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'down' in this phrasal verb, and 'shut' has a weaker secondary stress. In fast speech 'shut down' sounds like 'shu-DOWN.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it for businesses, factories, computers, and programs, and in news about schools or government closing. It is neutral but can carry a sense of abrupt or forced closure. For a phone or computer, you might say 'shut it down' or 'power down' in casual talk.

distinctions.note: Close down is more about ending a business permanently, while shut down often means stopping operation, which may be temporary.
Turn off is used for devices and lights; shut down is more often used for systems, businesses, or operations.

examples.everyday: The pizza place shut down for the winter, so we went somewhere else for dinner.
examples.professional: IT wants to shut down the old server tonight, so please save your work before six.
examples.analytical: The government's decision to shut down the agency raised questions about whether the policy would be reversed or permanent.

nuance.analogy: Think of a factory as a machine with a master switch: shut down means flipping that switch to bring everything to a stop.
common_mistakes: Using 'shut down' as a noun in place of 'shutdown' (e.g., 'a shut down' instead of 'a shutdown').
Placing the object after 'down' without 'it' in cases where a pronoun is needed: say 'shut it down,' not 'shut down it.'

conversation.text: Make sure you shut down your computer before you leave.
The factory shut down after forty years.
Every idea I suggested, she shut down.

senses.definition: (historical) A sacrificial offering of flour or an animal, commanded in the Torah (Leviticus 4.1-35), serving to atone for the unintentional transgression of a prohibition.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: A sacrifice of an animal or grain offered in ancient Israel under Mosaic law to atone for unintentional sins.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on AW in 'offering', and 'sin' has a weaker secondary stress. The r in 'offering' is clear in General American, and the final -ing is a light 'ing', not 'eeng'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and religious. It is a technical term for Bible study rather than an emotional word.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly use sin offering in Bible study, sermons and religious studies, and many ordinary speakers may never use it. It is written as two lowercase words. In a Bible study, a natural reply is 'Right, the priest offered it for unintentional sin.'

distinctions.note: A burnt offering was wholly burned as a gift to God, while a sin offering atoned for sin and some parts were given to priests.
A guilt offering dealt with wrongs that required restitution, while a sin offering covered sin in general.
A peace offering was a shared meal celebrating fellowship; a sin offering focused on atonement and cleansing.

collocations: the priest offers the sin offering
a sin offering for the people

examples.everyday: My Bible study group spent the evening reading about the sin offering in Leviticus.
examples.professional: In the seminar, we compared the sin offering with the ritual of the Day of Atonement.
examples.analytical: The sin offering in Leviticus 4 shows that unintentional violations required ritual cleansing before forgiveness.

nuance.analogy: A sin offering was like a repair payment after an accidental break, restoring what was damaged.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew chatta't, sin offering, from chata', to miss the mark.
common_mistakes: Writing it as one word, 'sinoffering'; standard writing keeps two words.
Treating it as a payment for any sin; the Torah assigned it mainly to unintentional sins.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew is chatta't (חַטָּאת), a sacrifice for sin, and it is central to the sacrificial system in Leviticus. Leviticus 4:3 describes a sin offering brought by a priest who has sinned unintentionally. Leviticus 4:35 says the priest makes atonement for the one who sinned, who is then forgiven. Hebrews 9:22 says that without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness, reflecting this sacrificial logic.

senses.definition: Initialism of social license to operate.
Initialism of service-level objective.

core.definition: Service-level objective: a measurable target for a system's performance, such as uptime or response time, used in reliability engineering.

pronunciation.tip: Americans say the letters one by one, 'S-L-O,' and do not say it as the word 'slow.' Stress the final letter O and keep the first two letters light.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term used among engineers and operations staff.
nuance.usage_note: In American tech teams, people spell this abbreviation out in standups, incident reviews, and dashboards. Saying 'slow' instead can confuse listeners. In a meeting, a typical phrase is 'Our SLO is 99.9 percent uptime.'

distinctions.note: An SLA, service-level agreement, is a contract with customers that may include penalties; an SLO is an internal target that is usually stricter.
An SLI, service-level indicator, is the measurement itself, while an SLO sets the target that the indicator should meet.

examples.everyday: My friend who works at a software company says their uptime SLO is basically the thing that keeps her awake at night.
examples.professional: We missed the SLO for latency this month, so we need to review the database indexes.
examples.analytical: A well-defined SLO balances reliability against the cost of engineering effort, making tradeoffs explicit.

nuance.analogy: Like a speed limit on a highway: it is a target you measure constantly to know whether the system is behaving.
nuance.etymology: An initialism of 'service-level objective,' formed from the standard reliability engineering vocabulary.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing SLO as the word 'slow.'
Confusing SLO with SLA, which is a legal contract.

senses.definition: A hollow tube, held in the mouth, or mounted on and opening into a diving mask, used by swimmers for breathing underwater.
senses.example: They wore snorkels while exploring the coral reef.

senses.definition: A retractable tube fitted in diesel-engine submarines to allow sufficient ventilation that the engines may be used at periscope depth.
A snorkel parka.
To use a snorkel.
senses.example: We spent the afternoon snorkeling in the clear blue waters.

core.definition: A breathing tube that you hold in your mouth while swimming face-down near the surface, so you can see underwater without lifting your head.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the r is strong and clear. The last syllable is a reduced "-kul", not "-kell".

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, everyday equipment word.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use "snorkel" for the tube worn with a mask on vacation, at the beach, or on a boat trip. As a verb, people say they "go snorkeling" rather than "snorkel around" in casual talk, though "snorkel" by itself is also natural. Snorkels are sold in sporting goods and beach shops and are often bundled with a mask and fins.

distinctions.note: Scuba uses a tank of compressed air to breathe underwater at depth; a snorkel only lets you breathe at the surface.
Diving usually means going underwater for a longer time, often deeper, with equipment; snorkeling stays near the surface.

examples.everyday: We rented a snorkel and mask at the beach shop, and the kids loved looking at the fish.
examples.professional: Our team offsite includes a snorkeling trip, so please bring your own swimsuit and sunscreen.
examples.analytical: The snorkel is a small device, yet it changes the swimmer's relationship to the sea, letting one observe without fully entering it.

nuance.analogy: A snorkel is like a periscope for a swimmer: a tube that lets you see and breathe while the rest of you stays underwater.
nuance.etymology: From German Schnorchel, a breathing pipe; the origin of the German word is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Saying "snorkle" without the e; the spelling includes "snork-" and "-el".
Saying "go snorkel" in casual speech; Americans normally say "go snorkeling."

conversation.text: Can I borrow your mask and snorkel?
My snorkel keeps filling up with water.
We snorkeled along the reef and saw a sea turtle.

senses.definition: The set of structures needed to reason about a given software system.

core.definition: The set of high-level structures of a software system, and the principles for reasoning about how its parts interact.

pronunciation.tip: Say SAWFT-wair as one smooth word, with stress on AR in architecture. Keep the r in both words, and reduce the middle vowels to a schwa in AR-kuh-tek-chur.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a professional term used in engineering teams and job titles.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'software architecture' in design reviews, job descriptions, and planning documents. A software architect makes high-level decisions about components, data flow, and deployment. The term is standard in tech companies, so use it in workplace conversation without explanation.

distinctions.note: System design often refers to a specific design interview or process; software architecture refers to the structures themselves and the reasoning behind them.
Software design usually covers detailed class and module decisions; architecture concerns the big structures and their quality attributes.

examples.everyday: My sister is a software architect, so she spends her days drawing diagrams for her team.
examples.professional: Before we add the new payment service, let's review the software architecture so the team agrees on the boundaries.
examples.analytical: A good account of software architecture explains not only the components but also the reasons for their trade-offs and constraints.

nuance.analogy: Like the blueprint of a building: it shows the rooms, the load-bearing walls, and the plumbing before anyone starts laying bricks.
nuance.etymology: Software from soft plus ware; architecture from Greek architektōn, master builder.
common_mistakes: Saying 'software architecture' with equal stress on every word; the stress falls on ARCH in architecture.
Confusing the term with 'software engineering' as a whole.

senses.definition: A bond of unity or agreement between individuals, united around a common goal or against a common enemy, such as the unifying principle that defines the labor movement; mutual support within a group.
senses.example: A long time union member himself, Phil showed solidarity with the picketing grocery store workers by shopping at a competing, unionized store.

senses.definition: Willingness to support another person in a difficult position or needs affection.
senses.example: Only the solidarity provided by her siblings allowed Margaret to cope with her mother's harrowing death.

core.definition: Unity among people who share a goal or face a common problem and support one another.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the DAIR syllable, which contains the r sound and the e vowel. The -ity ending is a reduced ih-tee, not 'ih-tay.'

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests loyalty, mutual support, and shared purpose.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use solidarity in news about protests, labor unions, social movements, and team support. People also say 'show solidarity with' someone facing a hard situation. It is widely understood but sounds more formal than everyday phrases like 'we've got your back.'

distinctions.note: Unity is general togetherness; solidarity implies a deliberate commitment to support others, often in a shared struggle.
Loyalty is faithfulness to a person or cause; solidarity is mutual support within a group facing a common situation.

examples.everyday: When my coworker's dad got sick, the whole office showed solidarity by bringing food and cards.
examples.professional: The data team stood in solidarity with the engineers during the scope debate so that neither group felt isolated.
examples.analytical: The author distinguishes solidarity, which rests on shared vulnerability, from charity, which can preserve distance between giver and receiver.

nuance.analogy: Solidarity is like a rope made of many strands: each one alone is weak, but together they hold a heavy load.
nuance.etymology: From French solidarité, from solidaire, from Latin solidus, whole or firm.
common_mistakes: Confusing solidarity with solid; solidarity is the abstract noun for unity.
Stressing the wrong syllable; the stress is on DAIR, not on the first or last syllable.

solidarity.etymology: By surface analysis, from English *solidary* + *ity*, or from French *solidarité* (“solidarity”), from *solidaire* (“characterized by solidarity”), from Latin *solidum* (“whole sum”), neuter of *solidus* (“solid”).

senses.definition: The direction or area lying to the south of a place.
Situated or directed towards the south; moving or facing towards the south.
Towards the south; in a southerly direction.

core.definition: Toward the south; in the direction of the south.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the ending -ward is unstressed and reduced to a short r-colored vowel. Do not add an extra syllable after the th.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use southward mainly in descriptions of movement, such as weather systems, migrating birds or routes on a map. In casual speech, people more often say 'south' alone, as in 'We drove south.' Southward is slightly more formal and descriptive.

distinctions.note: South is the everyday adverb for direction; southward is more descriptive and often appears in written or formal style.
Southerly describes wind or direction coming from or toward the south; southward describes movement toward it.

examples.everyday: The storm is slowly moving southward, so we might lose power tonight.
examples.professional: Our logistics team is shifting the warehouse inventory southward to the Atlanta distribution center.
examples.analytical: The author traces the migration of the tribe southward across the plains over several generations.

nuance.analogy: Like an arrow on a compass pointing down toward the bottom of the map.
nuance.etymology: From Old English sūth (south) and -weard (toward).
common_mistakes: Using 'southward' as a noun for the south; the noun is 'the south'.
Adding a syllable, saying 'SOWTH-ward-ayz' instead of ending with a reduced vowel.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word behind 'southward' is negeb (Hebrew נֶגֶב), meaning dry land or the south, the arid region south of Judah. Genesis 12:9 describes Abram journeying on by stages toward the Negeb. Genesis 13:1 says Abram went up from Egypt into the Negeb. These passages show the Negeb as a region of direction and movement in the patriarchal narratives.

senses.definition: Having widely spaced intervals.
senses.example: a sparse array, index, or matrix

senses.definition: Not dense; meager; scanty.
Having few nonzero elements.

core.definition: Having few nonzero entries, so most values in a dataset or matrix are zero.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a rhotic r, so pronounce the r clearly before the s. Do not add a vowel between the r and the s.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In general speech it can suggest a shortage or thinness, while in technical writing it is simply descriptive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sparse both in everyday speech for thinly spread things, such as sparse crowds or sparse furniture, and in data science and mathematics for data with mostly zero values. In technical talk, saying the data is sparse is a normal, precise description. For a general shortage, scarce is often more natural.

distinctions.note: Scarce means hard to find or in short supply, while sparse means thinly spread or not dense across a space or set.
Dense is the opposite: many items or nonzero values are packed close together.

examples.everyday: The town is sparse in the winter, so the diner is pretty quiet most days.
examples.professional: Our user-item matrix is very sparse, so we should use a sparse data format to save memory.
examples.analytical: A sparse signal is one in which most components vanish, and this assumption makes high-dimensional recovery possible.

nuance.analogy: A sparse matrix is like a parking lot where only a few spaces have cars and the rest are empty.
nuance.etymology: From Latin sparsus, past participle of spargere, meaning to scatter.
common_mistakes: Confusing sparse with scarce when talking about a general shortage.
Saying sparsy or sparsed instead of sparse.

senses.definition: To characterize as disgraceful or ignominious; to mark with a stigma or stigmata.

core.definition: To describe or treat a person, group, or condition as shameful or disgraceful, often unfairly.

pronunciation.tip: Stress on the first syllable. The middle syllable is a reduced 'uh', and the ending sounds like 'tize' with a long i.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it implies unfair judgment and harm to the person labeled.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'stigmatize' in discussions of social justice, health, and mental illness. It is formal and is most natural in writing or serious talk. In casual speech people say 'put someone down' or 'judge', but 'stigmatize' fits when the unfair social label is the point.

distinctions.note: Criticize means to judge something's flaws; stigmatize means to attach lasting shame to someone or a group.
Label is neutral; stigmatize implies a harmful, shaming label.

examples.everyday: I don't want to stigmatize anyone for needing a break from work.
examples.professional: Calling employees lazy for taking leave only stigmatizes people who need support.
examples.analytical: Labeling a whole community as criminal stigmatizes its members regardless of individual conduct.

nuance.analogy: Like a brand burned into skin, stigmatize leaves a mark that others see first.
nuance.etymology: From stigma with the suffix -ize, meaning to mark or treat as.
common_mistakes: Using 'stigmatize' as a synonym for 'criticize' in everyday contexts.
Mispronouncing the ending, saying 'stig-muh-tighz' with a long a sound.

senses.definition: A place built to withstand attack; a fortress.
A place of domination by, or refuge or survival of, a particular group or idea.
senses.example: the last stronghold of the Cornish language

core.definition: A fortified place built to resist attack; also a place where a group or idea is firmly entrenched and hard to dislodge.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the word is a compound with a secondary stress on hold. Don't add a vowel between the ng and the h, and pronounce the final d clearly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in military or history contexts; negative when describing a group's entrenched power or a bad habit, and positive when describing a refuge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use stronghold for a fortress in history or war, and figuratively for a place where a party, company or belief stays dominant, such as a city that is a political stronghold. In everyday talk you might say my dad's recliner is his stronghold. It is slightly literary, but common in news and sermons.

distinctions.note: A fortress is specifically a military building, while a stronghold can be any fortified place or a figurative base of power.
A refuge is a shelter from danger, whereas a stronghold can also be an aggressive base of power that resists outside control.

examples.everyday: My grandpa's recliner is his stronghold on Sunday afternoons, and nobody dares sit in it.
examples.professional: Our legacy billing system is still a stronghold for the finance team, so we can't retire it this quarter.
examples.analytical: Paul describes the arguments that resist the knowledge of God as strongholds that must be torn down, not merely debated.

nuance.analogy: A stronghold is like a castle on a hill: strong walls protect what is inside, and it is hard to take.
nuance.etymology: From strong plus hold, meaning a fortified place that can hold out against attack.
common_mistakes: Saying strongholt or stronghole, which mixes up the final sound; it ends in a clear d.
Using stronghold only for physical forts when Americans often use it figuratively for political or social bases.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word is metsudah or matsod, meaning a fortress or stronghold, and the Greek is ochyroma, meaning a fortified place. Psalm 18:2 calls the LORD David's fortress and stronghold, a place of safety. Psalm 144:2 describes God as the one who is my stronghold and my fortress. Second Corinthians 10:4 speaks of divine weapons able to destroy strongholds, meaning proud arguments that oppose the knowledge of God.

senses.definition: The element symbolically associated with hellfire or damnation, or in alchemy, the fiery principle present in all things.
A yellowish green color, like that of sulfur.
senses.example: sulfur:

senses.definition: Any of various pierid butterflies of the subfamily Coliadinae, especially the sulfur-colored species.
A chemical element with atomic number 16, having a bright yellow color and characteristic smell, used commercially in a variety of products such as insecticides, black powder, and matchsticks.
Of a yellowish green color, like that of sulfur.
Having a characteristic sulfur-like smell, reminiscent of rotten eggs.
To treat with sulfur, or a sulfur compound, especially to preserve or to counter agricultural pests.

core.definition: A pale yellow nonmetal chemical element with a strong smell when burned, used in matches, fertilizers, and rubber.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, SUL, and the final syllable is a reduced American r-colored 'er.' Many learners pronounce it with a separate 'ph' sound or stress the second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in science and industry; in religious or literary settings it can carry a dark, fearful sense.
nuance.usage_note: Americans spell it sulfur, not sulphur, which is the British spelling. In everyday speech, people might talk about the rotten-egg smell of sulfur, or the sulfur in matches. In Bible readings, the word is often translated brimstone, a term with strong associations with judgment and fire.

distinctions.note: Brimstone is an older English word for sulfur, used mainly in Bible translations and in sermons about hellfire.
Sulfurous describes something containing or smelling of sulfur, while sulfur is the element itself.

examples.everyday: The matches in that old box smell strongly of sulfur when you strike them.
